1	# Fall-detection design — wrap-up of floor-vibration cases
2	
3	This is the situation-by-situation design doc for the floor-vibration
4	fall detector. It assumes the sensing chain we have now (PVDF / PZT /
5	LIS3DH IMU on the floor → STM32 or ESP32 → host receiver → SNR GUIs).
6	
7	## Case 1 — separable: closest footstep < farthest fall
8	
9	> "The closest footstep vibration is smaller than the farthest falling
10	> vibration."
11	
12	This is the **easy case**. A single feature — peak |signal| or per-event
13	energy — splits the two classes with a margin. Implementation:
14	
15	- **Single-feature classifier.** SVM with a linear kernel on peak
16	  amplitude (or its log) is overkill — even a fixed threshold at the
17	  midpoint of the two distributions works.
18	- **Threshold selection.** Take the **maximum** observed close-range
19	  footstep peak as the noise ceiling, the **minimum** observed far-range
20	  fall peak as the signal floor, set the threshold at their geometric
21	  mean (or 1 standard deviation above the footstep ceiling).
22	- **Operating point.** Tune for high recall (catch all falls) at the
23	  cost of some FP — every missed fall is bad, false alarms are
24	  recoverable via a 30-second "are you OK?" prompt.
25	
26	If your real distributions look like this (one band of footsteps fully
27	below one band of falls with a clear gap), you're done. Most rooms with
28	short detection range, soft surface, and a well-placed sensor land here.
29	
30	## Case 2 — overlapping: closest footstep ≥ farthest fall
31	
32	> "The closest footstep vibration is bigger or equal to the farthest
33	> falling vibration."
34	
35	This is the **realistic case** for any deployment that has to cover a
36	real room — bedroom or bathroom — at ranges of 3–4 m. Amplitude alone
37	**will not** separate the classes, because a heavy bare-foot stomp 0.5 m
38	from the sensor really does deliver more peak energy than a light fall
39	4 m away. We have to use *waveform shape*, not just *waveform size*.
40	
41	### What is actually different
42	
43	| Feature | Footstep | Fall |
44	|---|---|---|
45	| **Duration above noise** | short, ~30–80 ms per footfall | longer, 100–500 ms (impact + body settle) |
46	| **Dominant frequency** | higher (foot/heel = small contact area, stiff coupling); typically 30–150 Hz | lower (soft body, larger contact area); typically 5–60 Hz |
47	| **Decay envelope** | quick, single-mode ring-down | longer, often **multi-stage** (hip strike → secondary impact from limb / head / shoulder over the next 100–300 ms) |
48	| **Repetition / cadence** | **periodic** at ~1.5–2.5 Hz (walking) or 2.5–4 Hz (running) | one-shot, no follow-up vibration of similar amplitude |
49	| **Pre-event activity** | usually preceded by other footsteps (the person walked here) | often preceded by footsteps that *stop abruptly* one footstep before the impact |
50	| **Post-event activity** | followed by more footsteps (walking continues) | **followed by stillness** for ≥ several seconds (the person is on the floor) |
51	
52	### Two-stage detector
53	
54	Build the detector as:
55	
56	1. **Event gate** — a simple amplitude/energy threshold. Low bar, just
57	   "something happened on the floor." Tuned to fire on the *smallest*
58	   thing we want to catch. This gate's output is a list of candidate
59	   events.
60	2. **Classifier** — for each candidate event, extract a feature vector
61	   over a ~500 ms window centered on the impact:
62	   - peak amplitude
63	   - total energy (∫ x² dt)
64	   - duration above noise (95th-percentile envelope)
65	   - dominant frequency + spectral centroid
66	   - band-energy ratios (0–20 Hz vs 20–100 Hz vs 100–500 Hz)
67	   - decay-envelope shape (fit `A·exp(-t/τ) + B·exp(-t/τ₂)`; τ₁/τ₂ ratio
68	     and the ratio of the two amplitudes capture the multi-stage signature)
69	   - **temporal context features** computed over the ±5 s window around
70	     the candidate:
71	     - count of preceding footsteps in last 5 s
72	     - count of following footsteps in next 5 s
73	     - time since previous footstep (long → "stopped abruptly")
74	
75	   Train a small classifier — Random Forest or Gradient Boosting on
76	   maybe 8–20 features works very well here and remains explainable.
77	   SVM with an RBF kernel works too. Don't reach for a deep network
78	   until you've shown a tree-based model can't separate the classes.
79	
80	   See **Appendix A — Feature dictionary** at the end of this document
81	   for definitions of each feature, what it physically captures, and
82	   why it helps separate footsteps from falls.
83	
84	3. **Post-event confirmation window** — once the classifier flags a
85	   candidate as "fall," **don't act yet**. Open a 5–15 s "stillness"
86	   window. If no footsteps occur during that window, raise the alarm.
87	   If a footstep does occur, downgrade to a near-miss / log only. This
88	   single gate reduces false alarms more than any feature-engineering
89	   trick because real falls really are followed by stillness.
90	
91	### Sensor strategies that help case 2
92	
93	- **More than one sensor.** Two sensors at opposite corners give you a
94	  rough difference-of-arrival, which corrects for distance: the *near*
95	  sensor sees a footstep, the *far* sensor sees ~0; a fall lights both
96	  up similarly. The amplitude *ratio* between sensors becomes a
97	  classification feature.
98	- **Pair the floor sensor with a low-rate IMU on a wrist or pendant.**
99	  Off-floor IMU + floor vibration is a very robust two-source confirmation
100	  even without a wrist-worn device, the IMU we just added (LIS3DH on
101	  the floor) is useful: it picks up tile-flexure modes that a piezo
102	  doesn't, and vice versa.
103	- **Per-sensor calibration per surface.** The detector that works on
104	  marble will fail on carpet; train one classifier per (sensor, surface)
105	  pair, then auto-detect surface at install via a known stimulus
106	  (the user is asked to "tap the floor near the sensor" once during
107	  setup).
108	
109	## How much energy counts as a fall (clinical threshold)
110	
111	> "How much energy should we consider as a fall? I assume an energy
112	> amount that would cause damage to an elderly."
113	
114	A useful framing: rather than picking an energy number out of the air,
115	anchor on the **biomechanical injury threshold for elderly**, then
116	back-solve for floor energy.
117	
118	### Injury thresholds from the literature
119	
120	- **Hip fracture (elderly, female, low BMD):** peak applied force at
121	  the greater trochanter of **~3,000–4,000 N** is the commonly cited
122	  threshold (Robinovitch et al., 1991; Yoshikawa et al., 1994). With
123	  an osteoporotic patient the threshold drops to ~2,500 N.
124	- **A typical sideways fall from standing** delivers
125	  **5,000–9,000 N** at the trochanter on a hard floor — comfortably
126	  above the fracture threshold. This is why falls from standing height
127	  are dangerous for the elderly.
128	- **The kinetic energy** at floor contact for a 60–70 kg adult falling
129	  from ~1 m of effective center-of-mass drop is roughly
130	  **300–500 J** (½·m·v² with v ≈ √(2gh) ≈ 4.4 m/s).
131	
132	### What we should target as our detector threshold
133	
134	We want to catch **any fall that has non-zero injury potential for an
135	elderly user.** That means erring well below the fracture threshold —
136	tripping and going to a knee from a sitting position is also a "fall"
137	worth recording, even if it doesn't fracture anything.
138	
139	A practical threshold for the *event gate* (Case 2 stage 1):
140	
141	- **Catch any floor-coupled impact equivalent to a 30 kg mass falling
142	  from 30 cm onto a hard surface.** That's ≈ **90 J input** (½ × 30 × √(2·9.81·0.3)²),
143	  of which something like 10–30 % couples into the floor as detectable
144	  vibration depending on the surface.
145	- This is well below a real human fall (300–500 J) so we keep recall
146	  high, and it filters out background "thumps" like dropping a phone
147	  (~5 J) or closing a kitchen drawer (~20 J).
148	
149	### How to actually calibrate this on your hardware
150	
151	Don't try to compute "energy at the sensor" directly — the
152	floor-to-sensor coupling is unknown and surface-dependent. Instead:
153	
154	1. **Drop a calibrated weighted bag** (e.g. a sandbag) from controlled
155	   heights onto the floor at varying distances from the sensor. This is
156	   a proxy for "fall energy" with known input joules.
157	2. **Record peak amplitude vs. (mass × height × distance)** for each
158	   surface / sensor combination. Fit a simple model.
159	3. **Set the event-gate threshold** at the peak amplitude that
160	   corresponds to your minimum-of-interest input energy at the
161	   *farthest* expected distance for that room.
162	
163	This calibration is the deliverable for Phase 2 in `water_drop_livingroom/EXPERIMENT.md`.
164	
165	## Case 3 — human fall vs. object fall
166	
167	> "How do we classify it as a human fall vs. things fall?"
168	
169	Both clear the event gate; both can have similar peak energies.
170	Classifying them apart needs features that exploit the *physics
171	difference between rigid and soft impacts.*
172	
173	### Physical differences
174	
175	| Property | Rigid object (book, phone, chair leg) | Human body |
176	|---|---|---|
177	| **Contact area** | small, well-defined | large, distributed (hip + thigh + shoulder over ~100 ms) |
178	| **Compliance** | low (rigid → high frequencies) | high (soft tissue → low frequencies) |
179	| **Impact duration** | short (~1–10 ms contact) | long (~30–100 ms contact, plus aftershocks) |
180	| **Spectrum** | broad, energy out to several hundred Hz | concentrated below ~50 Hz |
181	| **Number of impacts** | usually one (item drops, settles) | usually **multiple** (hip → arm → head over 100–500 ms) |
182	| **Impact location stability** | stationary after impact | the person may shift / try to get up over the next seconds |
183	| **Pre-impact context** | no footsteps immediately before | footsteps that **end abruptly** one step before |
184	
185	### Discriminating features (in addition to those in Case 2)
186	
187	- **Spectral centroid in the impact window.** Object falls land near
188	  100–300 Hz; human falls near 10–40 Hz. This is the single strongest
189	  discriminator on a properly-bandwidthed sensor (need ≥ 1 kHz sample
190	  rate and a wide-band sensor — the LIS3DH IMU is good for this; a
191	  bandpassed PVDF less so).
192	- **Multi-impact count in a 500 ms window.** Count the number of
193	  separate peaks above 0.3 × max in the event window. ≥ 2 is a strong
194	  human-fall hint; exactly 1 is a strong object-fall hint.
195	- **Pre-event footstep gap.** Bin the 5 s before the event into 250 ms
196	  slots; count slots that contain a footstep-shaped event. If the
197	  count is high in slots `[-5 s, -1 s]` and zero in the slot `[-0.5 s,
198	  0]`, that "footsteps stopped one step before impact" pattern is
199	  almost diagnostic of a fall.
200	- **Absence of "carry" signature.** People drop objects while walking;
201	  the dropping hand is moving, so the footstep cadence usually
202	  *continues* after the object drop. If footsteps continue with the
203	  same cadence within 1 s after the candidate event, downgrade
204	  strongly toward "object fall."
205	- **Amplitude vs. spectrum joint distribution.** A 90-J human fall has
206	  *smaller peak amplitude* but *more total low-frequency energy* than a
207	  90-J rigid drop. Joint feature: `peak_amp / low_band_energy` —
208	  small for human falls, large for rigid drops.
209	
210	### Decision pipeline for Case 3
211	
212	```
213	event detected
214	   │
215	   ├── compute features (peak, energy, duration, centroid, multi-peak count,
216	   │                     pre/post-cadence, band ratios)
217	   │
218	   ├── classifier 1: footstep vs. event-of-interest  (Case 2 model)
219	   │       │
220	   │       └── if footstep → log only, return
221	   │
222	   ├── classifier 2: human fall vs. object fall
223	   │       │
224	   │       └── if object fall → log only, return
225	   │
226	   └── enter post-event stillness gate (5–15 s)
227	           │
228	           ├── if footstep in window → likely false-positive human fall, downgrade
229	           │
230	           └── if no footstep → raise alarm
231	```
232	
233	Both classifiers can share the same feature extractor; only the
234	training labels differ. Training data needs three labelled classes:
235	**footstep** (huge, easy to collect), **object-fall** (deliberate
236	drops of varied items), **human-fall** (simulated falls onto a thick
237	mat with the same body mass and trajectory; ethically the only way to
238	get this without endangering a subject).
239	
240	## Open questions / next decisions
241	
242	1. **Sensor down-selection** has to come before classifier work — the
243	   feature set above assumes we have a wide-bandwidth sensor (LIS3DH at
244	   1 kHz looks promising). If we end up sensor-bandwidth-limited
245	   (e.g. PVDF + a 200 Hz LPF), the spectral-centroid feature collapses
246	   and we lean harder on temporal-context features.
247	2. **Multi-sensor or single-sensor?** Two sensors per room is much more
248	   robust for Case 2 but doubles the install cost. Worth a separate
249	   measurement campaign once Phase 2 is in.
250	3. **On-device vs. on-host classifier?** A small Random Forest fits in
251	   < 50 KB of flash and runs in < 1 ms on the ESP32-S3. The host can
252	   own training and the device runs inference. No real reason to push
253	   inference off-device unless we add a deep model later.
254	4. **Ground-truth collection strategy.** Simulated falls onto a mat are
255	   the only safe option. We'll need a short protocol document for
256	   recording them consistently — same drop heights, same body
257	   orientations, same distances from sensor. (Phase 4 in the
258	   livingroom experiment doc.)
259	
260	## Summary table
261	
262	| Scenario | Hardest sub-problem | Primary approach | Key feature(s) | Required hardware |
263	|---|---|---|---|---|
264	| Case 1 (separable) | none | fixed threshold or 1-feature SVM | peak amplitude | one sensor, any rate |
265	| Case 2 (overlapping) | distinguishing footsteps from far falls | 2-stage: event gate + multi-feature classifier + post-event stillness gate | spectral centroid, decay shape, footstep cadence, post-event silence | wide-bandwidth sensor (≥ 1 kHz), ideally 2 sensors per room |
266	| Case 3 (human vs. object) | small-mass-but-high-impact objects | physics-based features in a binary classifier following Case-2 | multi-peak count, low-band energy / peak amplitude ratio, pre-event footstep gap | wide-bandwidth sensor, large training set |
267	
268	The realistic deployment is **Case 2 + Case 3 stacked**: any room
269	covering 3–4 m needs the multi-feature classifier *and* the human-vs-
270	object stage *and* the stillness gate. Case 1 only applies inside
271	toilet-stall-sized footprints (which is actually a useful corner case
272	for the bathroom: cover only the 1.5 m around the toilet and the
273	problem becomes Case 1 + Case 3).
274	
275	
276	---
277	
278	# Appendix A — Feature dictionary
279	
280	This appendix defines the features used by the Case 2 (footstep vs.
281	fall) and Case 3 (human vs. object fall) classifiers. Each entry lists:
282	what the feature is, how to compute it, and what it physically captures
283	that helps separate the classes.
284	
285	## What "multi-feature classifier" actually means
286	
287	For each detected event, you compute a fixed-length list of numbers (the
288	**feature vector**) that summarizes the waveform's shape. You then feed
289	that list into a model that learned, from labelled examples, how to map
290	"feature vector" → "class label." The classifier is just a function that
291	turns ~10 numbers into a yes/no decision.
292	
293	A *single*-feature classifier looks at one number (e.g. peak amplitude)
294	→ a fixed threshold suffices. A *multi*-feature classifier looks at the
295	whole vector at once and learns rules like:
296	
297	> *high amplitude* AND *low dominant frequency* AND *long duration* → fall
298	> *high amplitude* AND *high frequency* AND *short duration* → footstep
299	
300	The classifier discovers the right combinations from the training data
301	— you don't hand-write them.
302	
303	## What "Random Forest / GBM" are
304	
305	Both are off-the-shelf machine-learning models in `scikit-learn`. They
306	learn the decision rules from labelled training data; you don't pick
307	the thresholds yourself. They're popular here because they are:
308	
309	- accurate without much tuning,
310	- fast (sub-millisecond inference, fit in < 100 KB of memory),
311	- explainable (you can ask "which feature mattered most?").
312	
313	| Model | One-line description |
314	|---|---|
315	| **Random Forest (RF)** | Builds many small decision trees on random subsets of the data and averages their votes. Robust, hard to overfit. |
316	| **Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM)** — `XGBoost` / `LightGBM` / scikit's `GradientBoostingClassifier` | Builds trees sequentially, each one correcting the previous tree's mistakes. Usually a few percent more accurate than RF, slightly more sensitive to overfitting. |
317	
318	For ~10 features and hundreds-to-thousands of training events, either
319	works. **Start with Random Forest.** Move to Gradient Boosting only if
320	RF plateaus and you've already collected more data; reach for a deep
321	network only if a tree-based model can't separate the classes at all
322	(it can, almost always).
323	
324	## Feature definitions
325	
326	For each candidate event, take a window of ~500 ms centered on the
327	impact peak and compute the following.
328	
329	### 1. Peak amplitude
330	
331	- **What:** `max(abs(signal))` over the event window.
332	- **Units:** g (for the IMU magnitude channel) or volts (for piezo).
333	- **Why it helps:** the easy case — when separable, this alone splits
334	  the classes. In the hard case it stops being decisive at long range,
335	  so we stack the rest of the features on top.
336	
337	### 2. Total energy
338	
339	- **What:** `sum(signal**2)` over the event window — the "size" of the
340	  event integrated over time, not just at the peak.
341	- **Units:** g²·s (or V²·s).
342	- **Why it helps:** falls deliver more *integrated* energy than
343	  footsteps even when peak amplitudes are similar — a fall's contact
344	  area is larger and the contact persists longer, so the area under the
345	  squared envelope is bigger. This catches "tall but narrow" footstep
346	  spikes and rejects them.
347	
348	### 3. Duration above noise
349	
350	- **What:** compute the signal envelope (Hilbert transform or rolling
351	  RMS over ~10 ms), then count the number of milliseconds the envelope
352	  stays above a threshold like `3 × noise_rms`.
353	- **Units:** ms.
354	- **Why it helps:**
355	  - footsteps: ~30–80 ms (one quick heel-strike + ringdown),
356	  - falls: 100–500 ms (impact + body settling + secondary impacts).
357	
358	### 4. Dominant frequency
359	
360	- **What:** take the FFT of the windowed signal, find the bin with the
361	  highest magnitude, report its center frequency.
362	- **Units:** Hz.
363	- **Why it helps:** physical contact mechanics:
364	  - footsteps couple through a small rigid contact (heel) →
365	    high frequencies (typically 50–200 Hz),
366	  - falls couple through soft tissue → low frequencies
367	    (typically 5–60 Hz).
368	- **Caveat:** only useful if your sensor and sample rate actually
369	  resolve those bands. PVDF behind a 200 Hz LPF preserves it; an
370	  audio-rate IMU is even better. A bandwidth-limited sensor collapses
371	  this feature.
372	
373	### 5. Spectral centroid
374	
375	- **What:** the magnitude-weighted average frequency of the FFT —
376	  `sum(f_i * |X_i|) / sum(|X_i|)`. A more robust cousin of
377	  "dominant frequency" because it doesn't latch onto a single bin.
378	- **Units:** Hz.
379	- **Why it helps:** captures the *overall tilt* of the spectrum — falls
380	  pull the centroid down even when no single bin dominates.
381	
382	### 6. Band-energy ratios
383	
384	- **What:** split the spectrum into a few bands (e.g. **0–20 Hz**,
385	  **20–100 Hz**, **100–500 Hz**) and compute the fraction of total
386	  energy in each band. With 3 bands you get 3 numbers that sum to 1.
387	- **Units:** dimensionless ratios in [0, 1].
388	- **Why it helps:** more discriminative than a single dominant
389	  frequency. Falls have most energy in the lowest band; footsteps
390	  spread it more evenly upward. Catches cases where the peak
391	  frequency happens to overlap (e.g. an 80 Hz footstep vs. a
392	  fall whose peak is also 80 Hz but with a fat low-frequency tail).
393	
394	### 7. Decay-envelope shape
395	
396	- **What:** fit a decaying exponential — or two stacked exponentials —
397	  to the post-peak signal envelope:
398	  ```
399	  envelope(t) ≈ A · exp(-t / τ₁) + B · exp(-t / τ₂)
400	  ```
401	  Report the two time constants `τ₁`, `τ₂` and the amplitude ratio
402	  `A / B`.
403	- **Units:** ms for τ; dimensionless for the ratio.
404	- **Why it helps:**
405	  - **footsteps**: single fast decay (one τ, ~10–30 ms),
406	  - **falls**: often a two-stage decay — initial big strike, then a
407	    smaller secondary bump 50–200 ms later when a limb / shoulder /
408	    head hits the floor. The two-time-constant fit captures that
409	    multi-impact signature even when the secondary bump isn't a
410	    separate detectable peak.
411	
412	### 8. Multi-impact peak count
413	
414	- **What:** in the event window, count the number of separate peaks
415	  whose amplitude is at least `0.3 × max_peak`, separated by at least
416	  20 ms.
417	- **Units:** integer count.
418	- **Why it helps (Case 3):** human falls almost always show ≥ 2 peaks
419	  (hip → shoulder → head, in some order, over 100–300 ms). Object
420	  falls usually show exactly 1.
421	
422	### 9. Footstep cadence in the ±5 s window (temporal context)
423	
424	- **What:** run the event detector over the 5 seconds *before* and 5
425	  seconds *after* the candidate event. Count footstep-shaped events on
426	  each side. Report:
427	  - **`pre_count`** — footsteps in `[-5 s, -0.5 s]`,
428	  - **`post_count`** — footsteps in `[+0.5 s, +5 s]`,
429	  - **`gap_pre`** — time from the most recent footstep to the candidate
430	    event (large value → "stopped abruptly"),
431	  - **`gap_post`** — time from the candidate event to the next footstep
432	    (large value → "didn't get back up").
433	- **Units:** counts and seconds.
434	- **Why it helps:** in real-world deployment this is the **most
435	  powerful** feature in the bag.
436	  - **Real human falls** look like: walk … walk … walk … BANG … silence
437	    (`pre_count` high, `gap_post` high).
438	  - **Footsteps** look like: walk … walk … STEP … walk … walk
439	    (`pre_count` and `post_count` both high, both gaps small).
440	  - **Dropped object while walking** looks like: walk … walk … BANG …
441	    walk … walk (`pre_count` and `post_count` both high → downgrade
442	    candidate to "object fall").
443	
444	### 10. Cross-feature ratios (derived)
445	
446	- **What:** combinations of the above that capture joint structure
447	  one feature alone misses. The two most useful:
448	  - **`peak_amp / low_band_energy`** — small for soft-body impacts
449	    (human falls), large for rigid impacts (object drops).
450	  - **`total_energy / peak_amp²`** — measures how "fat" the event is
451	    relative to a single-spike model. Falls have larger ratios than
452	    footsteps.
453	
454	## Worked example
455	
456	Two events both have peak amplitude = 0.50 g. Without more features,
457	a simple threshold can't tell them apart. Here's what the multi-
458	feature vector reveals:
459	
460	| Feature | Event A | Event B |
461	|---|---:|---:|
462	| Peak amplitude | 0.50 g | 0.50 g |
463	| Total energy | 0.012 g²·s | 0.080 g²·s |
464	| Duration above noise | 45 ms | 240 ms |
465	| Dominant frequency | 95 Hz | 18 Hz |
466	| Spectral centroid | 110 Hz | 35 Hz |
467	| Band ratios (low / mid / high) | 0.20 / 0.50 / 0.30 | 0.70 / 0.25 / 0.05 |
468	| Decay τ₁ / τ₂ | 18 ms / — | 25 ms / 110 ms |
469	| Multi-impact peak count | 1 | 3 |
470	| Footsteps in ±5 s | 8 (continuous walking) | 2 before (gap 0.4 s), 0 after |
471	
472	Trained on a few hundred labelled events of each class, a Random Forest
473	will reliably call **Event A → footstep, Event B → fall** — even though
474	peak amplitudes are identical. Case 2 solved.
475	
476	## Implementation notes
477	
478	- Compute features in Python with `numpy` + `scipy.signal` for FFTs and
479	  envelopes. The `analysis/snr_gui.py` and `analysis/peak_snr_gui.py`
480	  pipelines already produce most of the per-event numbers we need
481	  (peak, RMS, dominant frequency, duration); extending them to also
482	  emit band ratios and decay-fit parameters is a small change.
483	- For training: use `sklearn.ensemble.RandomForestClassifier`,
484	  start with `n_estimators=200, max_depth=8, class_weight="balanced"`.
485	  Track `feature_importances_` to see which features your model
486	  actually relies on — it'll usually flag spectral centroid, decay
487	  shape, and the temporal-context features as the heavy hitters.
488	- For deployment on the ESP32-S3: export the trained tree ensemble as
489	  C arrays via `m2cgen` or `emlearn`. Inference is a series of compares
490	  on the feature vector; runs in microseconds and fits in tens of KB.
491

# Fall-detection design — wrap-up of floor-vibration cases

This is the situation-by-situation design doc for the floor-vibration
fall detector. It assumes the sensing chain we have now (PVDF / PZT /
LIS3DH IMU on the floor → STM32 or ESP32 → host receiver → SNR GUIs).

## Case 1 — separable: closest footstep < farthest fall

> "The closest footstep vibration is smaller than the farthest falling
> vibration."

This is the **easy case**. A single feature — peak |signal| or per-event
energy — splits the two classes with a margin. Implementation:

- **Single-feature classifier.** SVM with a linear kernel on peak
  amplitude (or its log) is overkill — even a fixed threshold at the
  midpoint of the two distributions works.
- **Threshold selection.** Take the **maximum** observed close-range
  footstep peak as the noise ceiling, the **minimum** observed far-range
  fall peak as the signal floor, set the threshold at their geometric
  mean (or 1 standard deviation above the footstep ceiling).
- **Operating point.** Tune for high recall (catch all falls) at the
  cost of some FP — every missed fall is bad, false alarms are
  recoverable via a 30-second "are you OK?" prompt.

If your real distributions look like this (one band of footsteps fully
below one band of falls with a clear gap), you're done. Most rooms with
short detection range, soft surface, and a well-placed sensor land here.

## Case 2 — overlapping: closest footstep ≥ farthest fall

> "The closest footstep vibration is bigger or equal to the farthest
> falling vibration."

This is the **realistic case** for any deployment that has to cover a
real room — bedroom or bathroom — at ranges of 3–4 m. Amplitude alone
**will not** separate the classes, because a heavy bare-foot stomp 0.5 m
from the sensor really does deliver more peak energy than a light fall
4 m away. We have to use *waveform shape*, not just *waveform size*.

### What is actually different

| Feature | Footstep | Fall |
|---|---|---|
| **Duration above noise** | short, ~30–80 ms per footfall | longer, 100–500 ms (impact + body settle) |
| **Dominant frequency** | higher (foot/heel = small contact area, stiff coupling); typically 30–150 Hz | lower (soft body, larger contact area); typically 5–60 Hz |
| **Decay envelope** | quick, single-mode ring-down | longer, often **multi-stage** (hip strike → secondary impact from limb / head / shoulder over the next 100–300 ms) |
| **Repetition / cadence** | **periodic** at ~1.5–2.5 Hz (walking) or 2.5–4 Hz (running) | one-shot, no follow-up vibration of similar amplitude |
| **Pre-event activity** | usually preceded by other footsteps (the person walked here) | often preceded by footsteps that *stop abruptly* one footstep before the impact |
| **Post-event activity** | followed by more footsteps (walking continues) | **followed by stillness** for ≥ several seconds (the person is on the floor) |

### Two-stage detector

Build the detector as:

1. **Event gate** — a simple amplitude/energy threshold. Low bar, just
   "something happened on the floor." Tuned to fire on the *smallest*
   thing we want to catch. This gate's output is a list of candidate
   events.
2. **Classifier** — for each candidate event, extract a feature vector
   over a ~500 ms window centered on the impact:
   - peak amplitude
   - total energy (∫ x² dt)
   - duration above noise (95th-percentile envelope)
   - dominant frequency + spectral centroid
   - band-energy ratios (0–20 Hz vs 20–100 Hz vs 100–500 Hz)
   - decay-envelope shape (fit `A·exp(-t/τ) + B·exp(-t/τ₂)`; τ₁/τ₂ ratio
     and the ratio of the two amplitudes capture the multi-stage signature)
   - **temporal context features** computed over the ±5 s window around
     the candidate:
     - count of preceding footsteps in last 5 s
     - count of following footsteps in next 5 s
     - time since previous footstep (long → "stopped abruptly")

   Train a small classifier — Random Forest or Gradient Boosting on
   maybe 8–20 features works very well here and remains explainable.
   SVM with an RBF kernel works too. Don't reach for a deep network
   until you've shown a tree-based model can't separate the classes.

   See **Appendix A — Feature dictionary** at the end of this document
   for definitions of each feature, what it physically captures, and
   why it helps separate footsteps from falls.

3. **Post-event confirmation window** — once the classifier flags a
   candidate as "fall," **don't act yet**. Open a 5–15 s "stillness"
   window. If no footsteps occur during that window, raise the alarm.
   If a footstep does occur, downgrade to a near-miss / log only. This
   single gate reduces false alarms more than any feature-engineering
   trick because real falls really are followed by stillness.

### Sensor strategies that help case 2

- **More than one sensor.** Two sensors at opposite corners give you a
  rough difference-of-arrival, which corrects for distance: the *near*
  sensor sees a footstep, the *far* sensor sees ~0; a fall lights both
  up similarly. The amplitude *ratio* between sensors becomes a
  classification feature.
- **Pair the floor sensor with a low-rate IMU on a wrist or pendant.**
  Off-floor IMU + floor vibration is a very robust two-source confirmation
  even without a wrist-worn device, the IMU we just added (LIS3DH on
  the floor) is useful: it picks up tile-flexure modes that a piezo
  doesn't, and vice versa.
- **Per-sensor calibration per surface.** The detector that works on
  marble will fail on carpet; train one classifier per (sensor, surface)
  pair, then auto-detect surface at install via a known stimulus
  (the user is asked to "tap the floor near the sensor" once during
  setup).

## How much energy counts as a fall (clinical threshold)

> "How much energy should we consider as a fall? I assume an energy
> amount that would cause damage to an elderly."

A useful framing: rather than picking an energy number out of the air,
anchor on the **biomechanical injury threshold for elderly**, then
back-solve for floor energy.

### Injury thresholds from the literature

- **Hip fracture (elderly, female, low BMD):** peak applied force at
  the greater trochanter of **~3,000–4,000 N** is the commonly cited
  threshold (Robinovitch et al., 1991; Yoshikawa et al., 1994). With
  an osteoporotic patient the threshold drops to ~2,500 N.
- **A typical sideways fall from standing** delivers
  **5,000–9,000 N** at the trochanter on a hard floor — comfortably
  above the fracture threshold. This is why falls from standing height
  are dangerous for the elderly.
- **The kinetic energy** at floor contact for a 60–70 kg adult falling
  from ~1 m of effective center-of-mass drop is roughly
  **300–500 J** (½·m·v² with v ≈ √(2gh) ≈ 4.4 m/s).

### What we should target as our detector threshold

We want to catch **any fall that has non-zero injury potential for an
elderly user.** That means erring well below the fracture threshold —
tripping and going to a knee from a sitting position is also a "fall"
worth recording, even if it doesn't fracture anything.

A practical threshold for the *event gate* (Case 2 stage 1):

- **Catch any floor-coupled impact equivalent to a 30 kg mass falling
  from 30 cm onto a hard surface.** That's ≈ **90 J input** (½ × 30 × √(2·9.81·0.3)²),
  of which something like 10–30 % couples into the floor as detectable
  vibration depending on the surface.
- This is well below a real human fall (300–500 J) so we keep recall
  high, and it filters out background "thumps" like dropping a phone
  (~5 J) or closing a kitchen drawer (~20 J).

### How to actually calibrate this on your hardware

Don't try to compute "energy at the sensor" directly — the
floor-to-sensor coupling is unknown and surface-dependent. Instead:

1. **Drop a calibrated weighted bag** (e.g. a sandbag) from controlled
   heights onto the floor at varying distances from the sensor. This is
   a proxy for "fall energy" with known input joules.
2. **Record peak amplitude vs. (mass × height × distance)** for each
   surface / sensor combination. Fit a simple model.
3. **Set the event-gate threshold** at the peak amplitude that
   corresponds to your minimum-of-interest input energy at the
   *farthest* expected distance for that room.

This calibration is the deliverable for Phase 2 in `water_drop_livingroom/EXPERIMENT.md`.

## Case 3 — human fall vs. object fall

> "How do we classify it as a human fall vs. things fall?"

Both clear the event gate; both can have similar peak energies.
Classifying them apart needs features that exploit the *physics
difference between rigid and soft impacts.*

### Physical differences

| Property | Rigid object (book, phone, chair leg) | Human body |
|---|---|---|
| **Contact area** | small, well-defined | large, distributed (hip + thigh + shoulder over ~100 ms) |
| **Compliance** | low (rigid → high frequencies) | high (soft tissue → low frequencies) |
| **Impact duration** | short (~1–10 ms contact) | long (~30–100 ms contact, plus aftershocks) |
| **Spectrum** | broad, energy out to several hundred Hz | concentrated below ~50 Hz |
| **Number of impacts** | usually one (item drops, settles) | usually **multiple** (hip → arm → head over 100–500 ms) |
| **Impact location stability** | stationary after impact | the person may shift / try to get up over the next seconds |
| **Pre-impact context** | no footsteps immediately before | footsteps that **end abruptly** one step before |

### Discriminating features (in addition to those in Case 2)

- **Spectral centroid in the impact window.** Object falls land near
  100–300 Hz; human falls near 10–40 Hz. This is the single strongest
  discriminator on a properly-bandwidthed sensor (need ≥ 1 kHz sample
  rate and a wide-band sensor — the LIS3DH IMU is good for this; a
  bandpassed PVDF less so).
- **Multi-impact count in a 500 ms window.** Count the number of
  separate peaks above 0.3 × max in the event window. ≥ 2 is a strong
  human-fall hint; exactly 1 is a strong object-fall hint.
- **Pre-event footstep gap.** Bin the 5 s before the event into 250 ms
  slots; count slots that contain a footstep-shaped event. If the
  count is high in slots `[-5 s, -1 s]` and zero in the slot `[-0.5 s,
  0]`, that "footsteps stopped one step before impact" pattern is
  almost diagnostic of a fall.
- **Absence of "carry" signature.** People drop objects while walking;
  the dropping hand is moving, so the footstep cadence usually
  *continues* after the object drop. If footsteps continue with the
  same cadence within 1 s after the candidate event, downgrade
  strongly toward "object fall."
- **Amplitude vs. spectrum joint distribution.** A 90-J human fall has
  *smaller peak amplitude* but *more total low-frequency energy* than a
  90-J rigid drop. Joint feature: `peak_amp / low_band_energy` —
  small for human falls, large for rigid drops.

### Decision pipeline for Case 3

```
event detected
   │
   ├── compute features (peak, energy, duration, centroid, multi-peak count,
   │                     pre/post-cadence, band ratios)
   │
   ├── classifier 1: footstep vs. event-of-interest  (Case 2 model)
   │       │
   │       └── if footstep → log only, return
   │
   ├── classifier 2: human fall vs. object fall
   │       │
   │       └── if object fall → log only, return
   │
   └── enter post-event stillness gate (5–15 s)
           │
           ├── if footstep in window → likely false-positive human fall, downgrade
           │
           └── if no footstep → raise alarm
```

Both classifiers can share the same feature extractor; only the
training labels differ. Training data needs three labelled classes:
**footstep** (huge, easy to collect), **object-fall** (deliberate
drops of varied items), **human-fall** (simulated falls onto a thick
mat with the same body mass and trajectory; ethically the only way to
get this without endangering a subject).

## Open questions / next decisions

1. **Sensor down-selection** has to come before classifier work — the
   feature set above assumes we have a wide-bandwidth sensor (LIS3DH at
   1 kHz looks promising). If we end up sensor-bandwidth-limited
   (e.g. PVDF + a 200 Hz LPF), the spectral-centroid feature collapses
   and we lean harder on temporal-context features.
2. **Multi-sensor or single-sensor?** Two sensors per room is much more
   robust for Case 2 but doubles the install cost. Worth a separate
   measurement campaign once Phase 2 is in.
3. **On-device vs. on-host classifier?** A small Random Forest fits in
   < 50 KB of flash and runs in < 1 ms on the ESP32-S3. The host can
   own training and the device runs inference. No real reason to push
   inference off-device unless we add a deep model later.
4. **Ground-truth collection strategy.** Simulated falls onto a mat are
   the only safe option. We'll need a short protocol document for
   recording them consistently — same drop heights, same body
   orientations, same distances from sensor. (Phase 4 in the
   livingroom experiment doc.)

## Summary table

| Scenario | Hardest sub-problem | Primary approach | Key feature(s) | Required hardware |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Case 1 (separable) | none | fixed threshold or 1-feature SVM | peak amplitude | one sensor, any rate |
| Case 2 (overlapping) | distinguishing footsteps from far falls | 2-stage: event gate + multi-feature classifier + post-event stillness gate | spectral centroid, decay shape, footstep cadence, post-event silence | wide-bandwidth sensor (≥ 1 kHz), ideally 2 sensors per room |
| Case 3 (human vs. object) | small-mass-but-high-impact objects | physics-based features in a binary classifier following Case-2 | multi-peak count, low-band energy / peak amplitude ratio, pre-event footstep gap | wide-bandwidth sensor, large training set |

The realistic deployment is **Case 2 + Case 3 stacked**: any room
covering 3–4 m needs the multi-feature classifier *and* the human-vs-
object stage *and* the stillness gate. Case 1 only applies inside
toilet-stall-sized footprints (which is actually a useful corner case
for the bathroom: cover only the 1.5 m around the toilet and the
problem becomes Case 1 + Case 3).


---

# Appendix A — Feature dictionary

This appendix defines the features used by the Case 2 (footstep vs.
fall) and Case 3 (human vs. object fall) classifiers. Each entry lists:
what the feature is, how to compute it, and what it physically captures
that helps separate the classes.

## What "multi-feature classifier" actually means

For each detected event, you compute a fixed-length list of numbers (the
**feature vector**) that summarizes the waveform's shape. You then feed
that list into a model that learned, from labelled examples, how to map
"feature vector" → "class label." The classifier is just a function that
turns ~10 numbers into a yes/no decision.

A *single*-feature classifier looks at one number (e.g. peak amplitude)
→ a fixed threshold suffices. A *multi*-feature classifier looks at the
whole vector at once and learns rules like:

> *high amplitude* AND *low dominant frequency* AND *long duration* → fall
> *high amplitude* AND *high frequency* AND *short duration* → footstep

The classifier discovers the right combinations from the training data
— you don't hand-write them.

## What "Random Forest / GBM" are

Both are off-the-shelf machine-learning models in `scikit-learn`. They
learn the decision rules from labelled training data; you don't pick
the thresholds yourself. They're popular here because they are:

- accurate without much tuning,
- fast (sub-millisecond inference, fit in < 100 KB of memory),
- explainable (you can ask "which feature mattered most?").

| Model | One-line description |
|---|---|
| **Random Forest (RF)** | Builds many small decision trees on random subsets of the data and averages their votes. Robust, hard to overfit. |
| **Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM)** — `XGBoost` / `LightGBM` / scikit's `GradientBoostingClassifier` | Builds trees sequentially, each one correcting the previous tree's mistakes. Usually a few percent more accurate than RF, slightly more sensitive to overfitting. |

For ~10 features and hundreds-to-thousands of training events, either
works. **Start with Random Forest.** Move to Gradient Boosting only if
RF plateaus and you've already collected more data; reach for a deep
network only if a tree-based model can't separate the classes at all
(it can, almost always).

## Feature definitions

For each candidate event, take a window of ~500 ms centered on the
impact peak and compute the following.

### 1. Peak amplitude

- **What:** `max(abs(signal))` over the event window.
- **Units:** g (for the IMU magnitude channel) or volts (for piezo).
- **Why it helps:** the easy case — when separable, this alone splits
  the classes. In the hard case it stops being decisive at long range,
  so we stack the rest of the features on top.

### 2. Total energy

- **What:** `sum(signal**2)` over the event window — the "size" of the
  event integrated over time, not just at the peak.
- **Units:** g²·s (or V²·s).
- **Why it helps:** falls deliver more *integrated* energy than
  footsteps even when peak amplitudes are similar — a fall's contact
  area is larger and the contact persists longer, so the area under the
  squared envelope is bigger. This catches "tall but narrow" footstep
  spikes and rejects them.

### 3. Duration above noise

- **What:** compute the signal envelope (Hilbert transform or rolling
  RMS over ~10 ms), then count the number of milliseconds the envelope
  stays above a threshold like `3 × noise_rms`.
- **Units:** ms.
- **Why it helps:**
  - footsteps: ~30–80 ms (one quick heel-strike + ringdown),
  - falls: 100–500 ms (impact + body settling + secondary impacts).

### 4. Dominant frequency

- **What:** take the FFT of the windowed signal, find the bin with the
  highest magnitude, report its center frequency.
- **Units:** Hz.
- **Why it helps:** physical contact mechanics:
  - footsteps couple through a small rigid contact (heel) →
    high frequencies (typically 50–200 Hz),
  - falls couple through soft tissue → low frequencies
    (typically 5–60 Hz).
- **Caveat:** only useful if your sensor and sample rate actually
  resolve those bands. PVDF behind a 200 Hz LPF preserves it; an
  audio-rate IMU is even better. A bandwidth-limited sensor collapses
  this feature.

### 5. Spectral centroid

- **What:** the magnitude-weighted average frequency of the FFT —
  `sum(f_i * |X_i|) / sum(|X_i|)`. A more robust cousin of
  "dominant frequency" because it doesn't latch onto a single bin.
- **Units:** Hz.
- **Why it helps:** captures the *overall tilt* of the spectrum — falls
  pull the centroid down even when no single bin dominates.

### 6. Band-energy ratios

- **What:** split the spectrum into a few bands (e.g. **0–20 Hz**,
  **20–100 Hz**, **100–500 Hz**) and compute the fraction of total
  energy in each band. With 3 bands you get 3 numbers that sum to 1.
- **Units:** dimensionless ratios in [0, 1].
- **Why it helps:** more discriminative than a single dominant
  frequency. Falls have most energy in the lowest band; footsteps
  spread it more evenly upward. Catches cases where the peak
  frequency happens to overlap (e.g. an 80 Hz footstep vs. a
  fall whose peak is also 80 Hz but with a fat low-frequency tail).

### 7. Decay-envelope shape

- **What:** fit a decaying exponential — or two stacked exponentials —
  to the post-peak signal envelope:
  ```
  envelope(t) ≈ A · exp(-t / τ₁) + B · exp(-t / τ₂)
  ```
  Report the two time constants `τ₁`, `τ₂` and the amplitude ratio
  `A / B`.
- **Units:** ms for τ; dimensionless for the ratio.
- **Why it helps:**
  - **footsteps**: single fast decay (one τ, ~10–30 ms),
  - **falls**: often a two-stage decay — initial big strike, then a
    smaller secondary bump 50–200 ms later when a limb / shoulder /
    head hits the floor. The two-time-constant fit captures that
    multi-impact signature even when the secondary bump isn't a
    separate detectable peak.

### 8. Multi-impact peak count

- **What:** in the event window, count the number of separate peaks
  whose amplitude is at least `0.3 × max_peak`, separated by at least
  20 ms.
- **Units:** integer count.
- **Why it helps (Case 3):** human falls almost always show ≥ 2 peaks
  (hip → shoulder → head, in some order, over 100–300 ms). Object
  falls usually show exactly 1.

### 9. Footstep cadence in the ±5 s window (temporal context)

- **What:** run the event detector over the 5 seconds *before* and 5
  seconds *after* the candidate event. Count footstep-shaped events on
  each side. Report:
  - **`pre_count`** — footsteps in `[-5 s, -0.5 s]`,
  - **`post_count`** — footsteps in `[+0.5 s, +5 s]`,
  - **`gap_pre`** — time from the most recent footstep to the candidate
    event (large value → "stopped abruptly"),
  - **`gap_post`** — time from the candidate event to the next footstep
    (large value → "didn't get back up").
- **Units:** counts and seconds.
- **Why it helps:** in real-world deployment this is the **most
  powerful** feature in the bag.
  - **Real human falls** look like: walk … walk … walk … BANG … silence
    (`pre_count` high, `gap_post` high).
  - **Footsteps** look like: walk … walk … STEP … walk … walk
    (`pre_count` and `post_count` both high, both gaps small).
  - **Dropped object while walking** looks like: walk … walk … BANG …
    walk … walk (`pre_count` and `post_count` both high → downgrade
    candidate to "object fall").

### 10. Cross-feature ratios (derived)

- **What:** combinations of the above that capture joint structure
  one feature alone misses. The two most useful:
  - **`peak_amp / low_band_energy`** — small for soft-body impacts
    (human falls), large for rigid impacts (object drops).
  - **`total_energy / peak_amp²`** — measures how "fat" the event is
    relative to a single-spike model. Falls have larger ratios than
    footsteps.

## Worked example

Two events both have peak amplitude = 0.50 g. Without more features,
a simple threshold can't tell them apart. Here's what the multi-
feature vector reveals:

| Feature | Event A | Event B |
|---|---:|---:|
| Peak amplitude | 0.50 g | 0.50 g |
| Total energy | 0.012 g²·s | 0.080 g²·s |
| Duration above noise | 45 ms | 240 ms |
| Dominant frequency | 95 Hz | 18 Hz |
| Spectral centroid | 110 Hz | 35 Hz |
| Band ratios (low / mid / high) | 0.20 / 0.50 / 0.30 | 0.70 / 0.25 / 0.05 |
| Decay τ₁ / τ₂ | 18 ms / — | 25 ms / 110 ms |
| Multi-impact peak count | 1 | 3 |
| Footsteps in ±5 s | 8 (continuous walking) | 2 before (gap 0.4 s), 0 after |

Trained on a few hundred labelled events of each class, a Random Forest
will reliably call **Event A → footstep, Event B → fall** — even though
peak amplitudes are identical. Case 2 solved.

## Implementation notes

- Compute features in Python with `numpy` + `scipy.signal` for FFTs and
  envelopes. The `analysis/snr_gui.py` and `analysis/peak_snr_gui.py`
  pipelines already produce most of the per-event numbers we need
  (peak, RMS, dominant frequency, duration); extending them to also
  emit band ratios and decay-fit parameters is a small change.
- For training: use `sklearn.ensemble.RandomForestClassifier`,
  start with `n_estimators=200, max_depth=8, class_weight="balanced"`.
  Track `feature_importances_` to see which features your model
  actually relies on — it'll usually flag spectral centroid, decay
  shape, and the temporal-context features as the heavy hitters.
- For deployment on the ESP32-S3: export the trained tree ensemble as
  C arrays via `m2cgen` or `emlearn`. Inference is a series of compares
  on the feature vector; runs in microseconds and fits in tens of KB.

| **`min(far_falls) ≤ max(close_walks)`** OR gap < 6 dB | Case 2 (overlapping) | Multi-feature classifier (Appendix A in `FALL_DETECTION_DESIGN.md`). |

2 dB gap with 3 trials, a fourth trial probably erases it. 6 dB ≈ 2×
amplitude is a comfortable floor.

  pass.

  room.** From `EXPERIMENT.md`:
  - Marble (livingroom): 4 m
  - Hardwood (bedroom): 4 m
  - Bathroom tile: 3 m

  height, same bag orientation.
- Tag each drop with **ENTER** (`fall` event) — press the key the
  instant the bag hits.
- Save as `<surface>_far_falls.csv`.

### Optional — interpolation runs (recommended)

- **`<surface>_mid_walks.csv`** — walking at 2 m
- **`<surface>_mid_falls.csv`** — drops at 2 m
- **`<surface>_close_falls.csv`** — drops at 0.5 m (lets you confirm

```
Surface: ____________________  Sensor: __________   Date: ________

[ ] Sensor mounted, ground tied, receiver connected, port confirmed
[ ] Distance markers placed at 0.5 / 2 / max-range
[ ] Quiet baseline recorded (30 s, no activity) → noise_floor.csv

[ ] Session 2 — far falls, 10 drops at max range → far_falls.csv

```bash

| Source | n events | min peak | max peak | mean peak | median peak | std peak |

| close_walks | 40 | … | **A** | … | … | … |

- **A** = `max(close_walks.peak)` — the noisiest footstep you'll ever see.
- **B** = `min(far_falls.peak)` — the quietest fall you have to catch.

| Separation gap | Overlap fraction | What it means |
|---:|---:|---|

| 0 to +6 dB | 0 % | Case 1 with thin margin — re-test with more trials before committing; if margin holds with 20 trials per side, treat as Case 1 with the threshold at A + 1 σ_walks. |
| 0 to −3 dB | < 20 % | **Case 2 light.** Most events still separable; multi-feature classifier needed for the overlap region. |
| ≤ −3 dB | ≥ 20 % | **Case 2 hard.** Full multi-feature classifier + post-event stillness gate (Appendix A). |

Record the result per surface — different surfaces may land in
different cases.

## Quick plot to commit alongside the data

A single PNG that makes the result immediately legible:

```python
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from analysis.snr_gui import load_firewater
walks, _ = load_firewater("close_walks.csv", return_events=True)
falls, _ = load_firewater("far_falls.csv",   return_events=True)
# (Read peak values from the per_event peaks.csv files instead in practice.)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
ax.eventplot([np.log10(walk_peaks), np.log10(fall_peaks)],
             colors=["#1f77b4", "#d62728"], lineoffsets=[0, 1])
ax.set_yticks([0, 1]); ax.set_yticklabels(["close walks", "far falls"])

1	# Sensor mounting — PVDF, PVDF + proof mass, PZT
2	
3	How you mount each sensor matters at least as much as which sensor you
4	pick. The same chip on the same floor with two different mounts gives
5	different SNR, different bandwidth, and sometimes different *physics*
6	(strain sensor vs accelerometer). This doc covers the three sensor
7	configurations we're using.
8	
9	## TL;DR — the right mount for each, in one line
10	
11	| Sensor | Best mount | Sensing mode | Best at |
12	|---|---|---|---|
13	| **Bare PVDF film** | Bonded flat to the floor (or to a thin metal shim coupled to the floor) with rigid epoxy across the full footprint | Strain — picks up in-plane bending of the floor | Low-frequency floor flexure (1–200 Hz). Cheap. Bad on stiff floors. |
14	| **PVDF + proof mass** | Cantilever or simply-supported beam with the mass at the free end, base bolted (or stiff-epoxied) to the floor | Acceleration — inertial | Surface acceleration up to ~1 kHz. Best general-purpose option for fall detection. |
15	| **PZT disc / ring with proof mass** | Center-bolted or rigid-epoxied to the floor through the metal carrier shim, **inside a shielded enclosure** | Acceleration / strain (depends on geometry) | High sensitivity, high frequencies. Hard to insulate. |
16	
17	## Universal rules (apply to all three)
18	
19	1. **Couple it rigidly to the floor.** Anything compliant between the
20	   sensor and the floor (foam, soft tape, blu-tack, the carpet pile)
21	   acts as a mechanical low-pass filter. You want the sensor to *move
22	   with the floor*, not relative to it.
23	2. **Surface prep.** Clean the mounting area with isopropyl alcohol,
24	   let it dry. Skip the wax / polish layer that's on most marble and
25	   tile floors — it kills adhesion. For temporary deployments, a 50 mm
26	   square of double-sided tape over a degreased patch is acceptable;
27	   for a real run, a thin layer of cyanoacrylate (super glue) or
28	   2-part epoxy is dramatically better.
29	3. **Strain-relieve the cable.** The cable run from the sensor to the
30	   front-end is a microphone — it picks up vibration, drag, and
31	   triboelectric charge if it moves. Glue the first 10 cm of cable
32	   *to the same surface as the sensor* with a separate dot of epoxy
33	   so cable motion doesn't reach the sensor pads.
34	4. **Shield it.** Especially for PZT and bare PVDF (high source
35	   impedance). A grounded copper-foil enclosure — even a folded piece
36	   of kitchen aluminum foil tied to circuit GND — drops mains hum and
37	   nearby switching noise by 10–20 dB. The bad PZT noise floor in
38	   `water_drop_livingroom/EXPERIMENT.md` is a textbook example of what
39	   skipping this costs you.
40	5. **Same mount for the whole experiment.** If you're comparing two
41	   sensors or two surfaces, the mount has to be identical between
42	   recordings. A change in adhesive or torque can move the SNR by
43	   5+ dB on its own.
44	
45	## Bare PVDF film
46	
47	### What it actually senses
48	
49	PVDF film generates a charge proportional to the **strain** along its
50	length. When the floor flexes (bends), the surface fibers stretch and
51	compress, and a film bonded to the surface stretches and compresses
52	with them. This is why PVDF works best for **low-frequency,
53	large-deflection** events — it's a strain sensor, not an accelerometer.
54	
55	### Mounting
56	
57	- **Adhesive** (in order of preference):
58	  1. Thin layer of **2-part epoxy** spread across the entire film
59	     footprint — gives the best strain coupling, full bandwidth.
60	  2. **Cyanoacrylate (super glue)** — quick, almost as good as epoxy,
61	     more brittle long-term.
62	  3. **Double-sided polyimide / Kapton tape** — fine for a 1-day
63	     experiment, but the tape itself shears under high-frequency
64	     content above ~200 Hz, so you lose the upper band.
65	  4. **Avoid:** foam-backed tape, blu-tack, anything compliant.
66	- **Coverage:** the *entire* film must contact the surface uniformly.
67	  Air gaps under any part of the film mean that part of the film
68	  doesn't strain, reducing output (and in extreme cases adding
69	  resonances at the air-pocket frequency).
70	- **Orientation:** PVDF has an anisotropy axis (the "stretch axis"
71	  marked by the manufacturer). Mount with that axis aligned along the
72	  expected direction of largest strain — for floor-flexure detection,
73	  that's usually parallel to the longest unsupported span of the floor
74	  / tile.
75	- **Electrodes / leads:** the silver-printed electrodes are fragile.
76	  Use conductive copper tape with conductive adhesive, or a soldered
77	  wire on a gold-plated pad — never bend the lead near the electrode.
78	- **Sub-strate plate trick:** if direct epoxy to the floor isn't
79	  acceptable (e.g. a marble surface you can't damage), bond the PVDF
80	  to a **0.1–0.3 mm steel or aluminum shim** first, then epoxy the
81	  shim to the floor. The shim couples the floor strain into the film
82	  while letting you remove the assembly cleanly later. Don't go thicker
83	  than ~0.3 mm or the shim stops flexing with the floor.
84	
85	### Pitfalls
86	
87	- **Tape adhesion failure** is the most common silent killer. After
88	  the first few hard impacts the tape partially delaminates at the
89	  edges; SNR drops by 10–20 dB and you don't notice because the
90	  baseline still looks fine. Inspect the edges before each session.
91	- **Cable strumming.** A 50 cm dangling cable will pick up its own
92	  resonance (~10–30 Hz) every time the floor moves. Tape it down.
93	- **Triboelectric noise.** PVDF is also pyroelectric and triboelectric
94	  — touching the film with bare fingers, or moving the leads, generates
95	  spurious charge spikes. Don't handle during a recording.
96	
97	## PVDF with proof mass (PVDF accelerometer)
98	
99	This is the configuration used as `PVDF_mass_*` in
100	`water_drop_livingroom/`. Adding a small mass converts the sensor from
101	a *strain* device into an *inertial* device — the mass resists motion,
102	so when the floor accelerates the PVDF gets bent by the inertia of the
103	mass. Different physics, different mount.
104	
105	### Geometry
106	
107	Two common mechanical configurations:
108	
109	```
110	   Cantilever                         Simply-supported beam
111	  ───────────────                     ───────────────────
112	                                                 
113	   ┌─────────────────┐               ┌──────────────────────┐
114	   │     mass        │               │       mass            │
115	   │                 │               │                       │
116	   ╞═════PVDF════════╡<- free end    ╞═══════PVDF═══════════╡
117	   │                 │               │                       │
118	   ║║║║ base ║║║║║║║║                ║║║                  ║║║
119	   ║║║║║║ floor ║║║║║                ║║║       floor      ║║║
120	```
121	
122	- **Cantilever** (one end clamped, mass at the free end) — higher
123	  sensitivity per gram of mass, lower resonant frequency. Good for
124	  picking up floor accelerations < 200 Hz.
125	- **Simply-supported beam** (both ends clamped, mass in the middle) —
126	  stiffer, higher resonant frequency, lower sensitivity. Good when you
127	  want broader bandwidth and don't mind giving up some output.
128	
129	For a fall-detection use case (event content mostly < 100 Hz on stiff
130	surfaces, < 50 Hz on soft surfaces), **cantilever** is usually the
131	right pick.
132	
133	### Mounting the base
134	
135	The whole point is that the *base* moves with the floor and the *mass*
136	lags behind. So:
137	
138	- **Base coupling: as rigid as possible.** Two-part epoxy across the
139	  entire base footprint, or — better — a small machined aluminum block
140	  bolted (M3) into a threaded insert epoxied to the floor. Removable
141	  and dramatically more rigid than tape. For temporary work, full-area
142	  epoxy directly to a clean surface.
143	- **Don't pinch the PVDF where it transitions from base to free
144	  section.** The transition zone is a stress concentration; if epoxy
145	  squeezes into the active film area, sensitivity drops.
146	
147	### Choosing the mass
148	
149	- A heavier mass → larger PVDF deflection per g of acceleration → more
150	  output, but lower resonant frequency (more bandwidth limit) and more
151	  fragile.
152	- A typical sweet spot for fall-detection on a 25 mm × 8 mm × 28 µm
153	  PVDF strip: **2–10 g** brass or steel mass at the free end. Glue it
154	  on with the same epoxy used elsewhere in the assembly.
155	- The mass material doesn't matter much (density × volume = mass), but
156	  brass / stainless steel are easier to glue to than aluminum (which
157	  oxidizes).
158	
159	### Resonance
160	
161	A cantilevered mass + PVDF is a damped second-order system with a
162	resonance somewhere between 50 and 500 Hz depending on geometry. **You
163	want this resonance well above the band you care about** (so it doesn't
164	ring and color the response), but ideally not so high that you lose
165	all sensitivity in the 10–100 Hz fall band.
166	
167	- Tap-test it before mounting permanently: tap the mass with a pencil,
168	  watch the receiver's plot, look at the dominant frequency in
169	  `peak_snr_gui.py`. If it sits around 200–500 Hz, you're in a good
170	  spot. If it sits at 30 Hz, the mass is too heavy or the cantilever
171	  too long; trim something.
172	
173	### Pitfalls
174	
175	- **Resonance in-band.** If your cantilever rings at 40 Hz, every fall
176	  excites a 40 Hz tone that swamps the actual signal shape. Stiffen
177	  the cantilever (shorter arm or thicker substrate).
178	- **Mass falls off.** Use real epoxy, not super glue, for the mass-to-
179	  PVDF joint — it sees high stress at every impact.
180	- **The base is too compliant.** Tape-mounted bases give the mass and
181	  the floor common-mode motion, killing sensitivity. Epoxy or bolt.
182	
183	## PZT (with proof mass — the `PZT_ringmass` configuration)
184	
185	PZT is much more sensitive per unit deflection than PVDF, but it's:
186	- **brittle** (cracks under shock if not protected),
187	- **high source impedance** (so it picks up every nearby EMI source
188	  unless properly shielded),
189	- **mechanically rigid** (wants to be bolted or rigid-epoxied, not
190	  taped).
191	
192	### The standard form factor
193	
194	The most common cheap PZT element is a **piezo buzzer disc**: a brass
195	shim ~20–35 mm diameter with a ceramic disc bonded to one side. The
196	brass shim acts as the structural carrier (and one electrode); the top
197	of the ceramic is the other electrode. With a small mass added on
198	top of the ceramic, this becomes the `ringmass` accelerometer.
199	
200	### Mounting
201	
202	- **Center-bolt** through the brass shim into a threaded hole or insert
203	  in the floor / a coupling block. Torque just enough to make the
204	  joint solid (~0.2 N·m); over-torquing crushes the ceramic.
205	- If you can't drill: **rigid epoxy** the brass shim to the floor
206	  across its full footprint. Don't tape — PZT mounted on tape rings
207	  uncontrollably and the response is dominated by the tape, not the
208	  floor.
209	- The mass sits on top of the ceramic, glued with epoxy. Same as PVDF:
210	  match mass to the bandwidth you need.
211	
212	### Shielding (the part that matters most)
213	
214	Skipping this is exactly what cost the PZT 16.5 dB of noise floor in
215	`water_drop_livingroom/EXPERIMENT.md`. Don't repeat the mistake.
216	
217	- **Coax cable from sensor to front-end.** Even 30 cm of unshielded
218	  twisted pair will pick up enough hum to bury small signals. RG-178
219	  or any audio-grade thin coax is fine. Solder the shield to circuit
220	  GND only at the front-end side (not at the sensor side) to avoid
221	  ground loops.
222	- **Faraday cage around the sensor.** Wrap the sensor + the first
223	  10 cm of cable in **copper or aluminum foil**, connect the foil to
224	  circuit GND via a short pigtail at the front-end side. Leave a
225	  small access hole only for the cable. The cage doesn't need to
226	  touch the ceramic — air gap is fine — but it must completely
227	  enclose it.
228	- **Front-end input impedance matching.** The PZT's source impedance
229	  is typically 100 kΩ – 10 MΩ at the frequencies of interest. A
230	  charge-amplifier topology (op-amp with a feedback capacitor) is the
231	  textbook front-end. A simple voltage buffer with an LMC6041 or
232	  AD8541 (FET-input, low bias current) also works for large signals.
233	  Don't drive a long cable directly out of the PZT.
234	- **Don't share ground with switchers.** The Pi's USB / 5 V regulator
235	  is a noise source. Run the PZT analog ground separately and merge it
236	  to digital ground at one star point at the front-end — never inside
237	  the PZT enclosure.
238	
239	### Pitfalls
240	
241	- **Cracking under impact.** PZT can survive shock if it's mounted
242	  with strain relief at the lead joints and the mass isn't slamming
243	  into the ceramic edge. After every hard test, inspect for new
244	  cracks (use a magnifier and look for hairlines around the brass-
245	  ceramic perimeter).
246	- **The ceramic is poled** — the polarity of the output depends on
247	  which electrode you pick as ground. If the trace looks "upside
248	  down" relative to the impact, swap the leads.
249	- **Resonant ringing.** PZT discs have very high-Q resonances
250	  (hundreds of Hz to a few kHz). If you see a single tone coloring
251	  every event, you're near a resonance — add a small damping mass or
252	  a viscous adhesive layer between the ceramic and the proof mass.
253	
254	## Mounting decision matrix
255	
256	If you just need to pick a mount in 60 seconds:
257	
258	| You have… | …on this surface | Mount choice |
259	|---|---|---|
260	| Bare PVDF film | wood / vinyl (compliant) | full-area epoxy direct to floor |
261	| Bare PVDF film | marble / tile (stiff) | epoxy to a 0.2 mm shim, then epoxy shim to floor |
262	| PVDF + mass | any | cantilever, base epoxied (or M3-bolted) to floor; tape only for first-pass test |
263	| PZT + mass | any | brass shim epoxied to floor, full Faraday cage + coax to front-end; M3-bolted if drilling allowed |
264	| Anything | a floor you cannot damage | shim + repositionable adhesive (3M VHB tape) accepting ~5 dB SNR loss |
265	
266	## Verifying the mount before recording
267	
268	A 30-second sanity check before every session:
269	
270	1. **Tap test.** Tap the floor 30 cm from the sensor with a pencil
271	   eraser. Live trace should show a clean, fast-decay impulse with a
272	   ringdown shorter than ~50 ms. If it rings for hundreds of ms or
273	   shows multiple harmonic peaks, the mount is resonating — re-mount.
274	2. **Knuckle test.** Knock once on the floor. The trace should hit a
275	   peak quickly and decay. If the peak is delayed (visible "rise"
276	   instead of an instant onset), the mount is compliant — re-mount.
277	3. **Hum test.** With everything connected but no mechanical input,
278	   look at the noise floor. Touch the cable shield; if the noise jumps
279	   markedly, your shield isn't grounded properly. Touch the sensor;
280	   if it spikes, you don't have a Faraday cage on a high-impedance
281	   sensor (PVDF / PZT).
282	4. **Repeat after the first hard impact.** Adhesive bonds settle (and
283	   sometimes partially fail) on the first big shock. Re-do the tap
284	   test after the first 2–3 fall surrogates.
285	
286	If all four pass, the mount is good. If any fail, fix it before
287	recording — you can't fix bad coupling in software.

# Sensor mounting — PVDF, PVDF + proof mass, PZT

How you mount each sensor matters at least as much as which sensor you
pick. The same chip on the same floor with two different mounts gives
different SNR, different bandwidth, and sometimes different *physics*
(strain sensor vs accelerometer). This doc covers the three sensor
configurations we're using.

## TL;DR — the right mount for each, in one line

| Sensor | Best mount | Sensing mode | Best at |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Bare PVDF film** | Bonded flat to the floor (or to a thin metal shim coupled to the floor) with rigid epoxy across the full footprint | Strain — picks up in-plane bending of the floor | Low-frequency floor flexure (1–200 Hz). Cheap. Bad on stiff floors. |
| **PVDF + proof mass** | Cantilever or simply-supported beam with the mass at the free end, base bolted (or stiff-epoxied) to the floor | Acceleration — inertial | Surface acceleration up to ~1 kHz. Best general-purpose option for fall detection. |
| **PZT disc / ring with proof mass** | Center-bolted or rigid-epoxied to the floor through the metal carrier shim, **inside a shielded enclosure** | Acceleration / strain (depends on geometry) | High sensitivity, high frequencies. Hard to insulate. |

## Universal rules (apply to all three)

1. **Couple it rigidly to the floor.** Anything compliant between the
   sensor and the floor (foam, soft tape, blu-tack, the carpet pile)
   acts as a mechanical low-pass filter. You want the sensor to *move
   with the floor*, not relative to it.
2. **Surface prep.** Clean the mounting area with isopropyl alcohol,
   let it dry. Skip the wax / polish layer that's on most marble and
   tile floors — it kills adhesion. For temporary deployments, a 50 mm
   square of double-sided tape over a degreased patch is acceptable;
   for a real run, a thin layer of cyanoacrylate (super glue) or
   2-part epoxy is dramatically better.
3. **Strain-relieve the cable.** The cable run from the sensor to the
   front-end is a microphone — it picks up vibration, drag, and
   triboelectric charge if it moves. Glue the first 10 cm of cable
   *to the same surface as the sensor* with a separate dot of epoxy
   so cable motion doesn't reach the sensor pads.
4. **Shield it.** Especially for PZT and bare PVDF (high source
   impedance). A grounded copper-foil enclosure — even a folded piece
   of kitchen aluminum foil tied to circuit GND — drops mains hum and
   nearby switching noise by 10–20 dB. The bad PZT noise floor in
   `water_drop_livingroom/EXPERIMENT.md` is a textbook example of what
   skipping this costs you.
5. **Same mount for the whole experiment.** If you're comparing two
   sensors or two surfaces, the mount has to be identical between
   recordings. A change in adhesive or torque can move the SNR by
   5+ dB on its own.

## Bare PVDF film

### What it actually senses

PVDF film generates a charge proportional to the **strain** along its
length. When the floor flexes (bends), the surface fibers stretch and
compress, and a film bonded to the surface stretches and compresses
with them. This is why PVDF works best for **low-frequency,
large-deflection** events — it's a strain sensor, not an accelerometer.

### Mounting

- **Adhesive** (in order of preference):
  1. Thin layer of **2-part epoxy** spread across the entire film

  2. **Cyanoacrylate (super glue)** — quick, almost as good as epoxy,

  3. **Double-sided polyimide / Kapton tape** — fine for a 1-day

- **Orientation:** PVDF has an anisotropy axis (the "stretch axis"

- **Sub-strate plate trick:** if direct epoxy to the floor isn't

This is the configuration used as `PVDF_mass_*` in

```

  ───────────────                     ───────────────────
                                                 
   ┌─────────────────┐               ┌──────────────────────┐

   │                 │               │                       │
   ╞═════PVDF════════╡<- free end    ╞═══════PVDF═══════════╡
   │                 │               │                       │
   ║║║║ base ║║║║║║║║                ║║║                  ║║║

- **Simply-supported beam** (both ends clamped, mass in the middle) —

- **Mass falls off.** Use real epoxy, not super glue, for the mass-to-

- **The base is too compliant.** Tape-mounted bases give the mass and

## PZT (with proof mass — the `PZT_ringmass` configuration)

- **brittle** (cracks under shock if not protected),
- **high source impedance** (so it picks up every nearby EMI source

  across its full footprint. Don't tape — PZT mounted on tape rings

- The mass sits on top of the ceramic, glued with epoxy. Same as PVDF:

### Shielding (the part that matters most)

Skipping this is exactly what cost the PZT 16.5 dB of noise floor in

- **Coax cable from sensor to front-end.** Even 30 cm of unshielded

| PVDF + mass | any | cantilever, base epoxied (or M3-bolted) to floor; tape only for first-pass test |
| PZT + mass | any | brass shim epoxied to floor, full Faraday cage + coax to front-end; M3-bolted if drilling allowed |
| Anything | a floor you cannot damage | shim + repositionable adhesive (3M VHB tape) accepting ~5 dB SNR loss |

## Verifying the mount before recording

A 30-second sanity check before every session:

1. **Tap test.** Tap the floor 30 cm from the sensor with a pencil
   eraser. Live trace should show a clean, fast-decay impulse with a
   ringdown shorter than ~50 ms. If it rings for hundreds of ms or
   shows multiple harmonic peaks, the mount is resonating — re-mount.
2. **Knuckle test.** Knock once on the floor. The trace should hit a
   peak quickly and decay. If the peak is delayed (visible "rise"
   instead of an instant onset), the mount is compliant — re-mount.
3. **Hum test.** With everything connected but no mechanical input,
   look at the noise floor. Touch the cable shield; if the noise jumps
   markedly, your shield isn't grounded properly. Touch the sensor;
   if it spikes, you don't have a Faraday cage on a high-impedance
   sensor (PVDF / PZT).
4. **Repeat after the first hard impact.** Adhesive bonds settle (and
   sometimes partially fail) on the first big shock. Re-do the tap
   test after the first 2–3 fall surrogates.

If all four pass, the mount is good. If any fail, fix it before
recording — you can't fix bad coupling in software.

# PVDF Piezoelectric Acquisition — Reproduction Guide

A step-by-step guide to rebuilding the two boards (**Design #1: single-channel + STM32 + OLED**, and **Design #2: 10-channel analog front-end**) and the firmware from the files in this repository.

> Everything you need is already in the repo: schematics, Gerbers, LCEDA source, BOM, and firmware. This document only describes the process for turning those files into working hardware.

Estimated time (first build, one person):
- PCB order + delivery: **5–10 days**
- Parts order: **3–10 days** (parallel)
- Assembly + bring-up of both boards: **~1 full day**
- Firmware flash + first light: **~30 minutes**

---

## 0. Skills & Tools Required

**Skills**
- SMD soldering down to 0603 / SOIC-8 / SOT-23-8 / LQFP-48 (fine-pitch ≥ 0.5 mm).
- Reading schematics + BOMs, using a DMM and oscilloscope.
- Keil MDK / ST-Link / J-Link usage for STM32.

**Bench tools**
- Temperature-controlled soldering iron (≈ 320 °C, fine tip).
- Hot-air rework station (for SOT-23-8 MP2315 and any rework).
- Tweezers, flux, 0.3–0.5 mm leaded solder, IPA + brush.
- Digital multimeter, ideally with µA range.
- Oscilloscope (≥ 20 MHz BW, 1× / 10× probes).
- Bench PSU (±15 V capable for Design #2; 12 V / 1 A for Design #1).
- ST-Link V2 (or J-Link) for STM32 flashing.
- USB-to-UART adapter (CH340, CP2102, or the on-board CH340 of the Alientek "Warship" dev board).

**Software**
- Keil MDK-ARM (free size-limited edition works; project is < 32 KB).
- ST Standard Peripheral Library (already bundled under `采集代码/STM32F10x_FWLib/`).
- Optional: LCEDA / EasyEDA (to open the `*.json` sources), Multisim 14 (for `陷波器仿真.ms14`).

---

## 1. Order the PCBs

Both boards were designed in **LCEDA (EasyEDA / 嘉立创 EDA)**. The simplest path is to upload the provided Gerbers to a Chinese prototype house (JLCPCB, PCBWay) or any fab of your choice.

### 1.1 Design #1 — single-channel + MCU + OLED
- **Gerber zip:** `PVDF压电采集资料/PVDF压电采集系统资料/Gerber_PCB_PVDF压电信号调理系统.zip`
- Recommended fab settings: 2 layers, 1.6 mm FR-4, 1 oz copper, HASL or ENIG finish.
- Approximate size: fits within 100 × 80 mm (confirm by opening the zip; LCEDA free-quota friendly).

### 1.2 Design #2 — 10-channel analog
- **Gerber zip:** `PVDF压电采集资料/10路PVDF采集/Gerber_PCB_10通道PVDF采集调理电路.zip`
- Same settings. ENIG is preferable on this board because of the 100 MΩ feedback node — clean immersion-gold pads leak less.

### 1.3 (Optional) Edit the design first

If you want to change anything before fabbing, open the LCEDA JSON sources:

| Board | Schematic JSON | PCB JSON |
|-------|----------------|----------|
| #1 | `PVDF压电采集资料/PVDF压电采集系统资料/PVDF压电信号调理系统/PVDF压电信号调理系统.json` | `…/PCB_PVDF压电信号调理系统.json` |
| #2 | `PVDF压电采集资料/10路PVDF采集/电路设计源文件/10通道PVDF采集调理电路.json` | `…/PCB_10通道PVDF采集调理电路.json` |

Open at https://lceda.cn/ (or https://easyeda.com) → File → Open → "EasyEDA Source" → pick the JSON.

---

## 2. Bill of Materials

### 2.1 Design #1 — single-channel board

Source of truth: `PVDF压电采集资料/PVDF压电采集系统资料/BOM_PVDF压电信号调理系统_2023-02-20.csv` (UTF-16; open with Excel/LibreOffice).

**Summary (57 line items):**

| Category | Items |
|----------|-------|
| **Protection / switch** | SMAJ12A TVS (D1); MSS22D18G2 slide switch (K1); DC-470-2.1GP barrel jack (J1) |
| **Power** | MP2315 buck (U2); AMS1117-3.3 LDO (U3); 4.7 µH 0630 inductor (L1); 22 µF, 100 µF, 10 µF bulk caps |
| **MCU + clock** | STM32F103C8T6 LQFP-48 (U15); 8 MHz SMD crystal (X2); 22 pF, 0.1 µF decoupling |
| **Analog** | MAX44248 dual (U1); TL072 (U14); LF353 ×2 (U8, U13); OP07 (U9); LM311 (U16) |
| **Precision R** | **100 MΩ 2512 (R48)** — the critical one; 100 k multi-turn trimpots RP2–RP5; 91 k, 43 k, 40.2 k, 20 k, 9.09 k, 7.5 k, 5.1 k, 5 k, 4.7 k, 3.3 k, 2 k, 1 k, 600 Ω, 510 Ω, 100 Ω, 10 Ω |
| **Passives** | 33 nF filter caps (8×); 22 µF, 100 µF, 10 µF, 1 µF (105), 0.2 µF, 0.1 µF (104), 33 pF, 22 pF |
| **User I/O** | 0.96″ I²C OLED SSD1306 (P1, 4-pin); green LEDs (LED1, LED4, LED5); tactile switches KEY2, KEY4 |
| **Connectors** | 2.54 mm headers 1×2, 1×3, 1×4, 1×6 (H0 – H16) |

**Key "don't-substitute" parts** (listed by LCSC code where possible so you can one-click order):

| Part | LCSC | Why it matters |
|------|------|----------------|
| STM32F103C8T6 | C8734 | Firmware is pin-compatible only with this exact MCU |
| MAX44248ASA+T | C92065 | Front-end noise floor; generic substitutes will degrade performance |
| OP07CSZ | C15360 | Low offset needed for the final gain stage |
| LM311DR | C12597 | Trigger comparator; any LM311 is OK |
| TL072IDR | C6962 | Generic; any TL072/TL082 works |
| LF353DR | C7918 | Generic; any LF353 works |
| MP2315 | C990008518 | Use this exact part for the given FB resistor values |
| AMS1117-3.3 | C6186 | Generic |
| HCNR200-500E | (in BOM, not drawn) | Optional isolation IC — skip unless you add an isolated output |
| 100 MΩ 2512 | — | **Critical**: don't downgrade to 0805 thick-film — leakage dominates |

External supply needed at H0: **±5 V** (the board does not generate the negative rail). Use a small ±5 V linear brick or derive from a bench PSU.
