skills.content:
Declare a Judicial Hearing or draft a Bill under the Crucible Constitutional Governance system.

Usage: /judicial <hear|bill> [args]

Subcommands:
  hear "<name>" <position-A> vs <position-B>   — declare and run a Judicial Hearing
  bill <problem description>                    — produce a complete, debate-ready Bill

Examples:
  /judicial hear "step trigger" "acc-primary peak" vs "gyr-primary push-off crossing"
  /judicial hear "BLE MTU vs USB CDC" "BLE NUS primary — matches production path" vs "USB CDC primary — deterministic"
  /judicial hear "Arduino vs Zephyr re-evaluation" "unblock Zephyr — new overlay evidence" vs "keep Arduino — block stands"
  /judicial bill step detection fails on stairs — acc_filt peak delayed by 80ms under sigmoid loading
  /judicial bill replace soft TPU enclosure — heel-strike transient attenuated below detection threshold

If no subcommand given, print this usage and stop.

---

## hear subcommand

Declares and runs a full Judicial Hearing. Implements CONSTITUTION.md Judicial Process §1–5.

### Step 1 — Warm the courtroom

Invoke the judicial-clerk agent immediately. It will:
- Verify agent roster (attorney-A, attorney-B, simulator-operator, plotter, uart-reader)
- Print COURTROOM READY before any argument begins

Do not proceed past Step 1 until judicial-clerk prints COURTROOM READY.

### Step 2 — Print hearing declaration

```
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
JUDICIAL HEARING DECLARED
Hearing: <hearing name>
Position A: <position-A-description>
Position B: <position-B-description>

Constitutional grounding to check before arguing:
  docs/governance/amendments.md          — all ratified amendments
  docs/governance/case_law.md            — all recorded precedents
  CONSTITUTION.md Judicial Process §3–4  — Benjamin Franklin + Thomas Jefferson principles

Evidence base to read before arguing:
  docs/device_context.md                 — BOM, circuit notes, test results, signal measurements
  docs/toolchain_config.md               — active hardware, pin map, blocked toolchains, repo registry

Evidence commands available during this hearing:
  /plot evidence signal <profile>         — IMU signal plot
  /plot evidence sim <profile>            — full simulation evidence (UART + signal)
  /plot evidence uart <log_path>          — UART session output from Renode log
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
```

### Step 2b — Advisory pre-brief (optional but recommended)

If the hearing topic involves algorithm or firmware logic:
  Suggest: "Run `/advisor sw detect` (or relevant focus) before attorneys argue."

If the hearing topic involves hardware, BOM, or enclosure:
  Suggest: "Run `/advisor hw` before attorneys argue."

### Step 3 — Assign attorneys and launch arguments (parallel)

Assign Attorney-A to Position A and Attorney-B to Position B (or reverse).
Launch both attorney agents in parallel. Each must:
1. Read docs/governance/amendments.md
2. Read docs/governance/case_law.md
3. Read docs/device_context.md — BOM, circuit notes, test results, signal measurements
4. Read docs/toolchain_config.md — hardware record and blocked toolchains
5. Read any source files directly relevant to their position
6. Present all four required argument elements:
   - Amendment(s) invoked (exact number and title)
   - Precedent (case name and date, or explicit statement of none)
   - Physical/clinical outcome protected
   - Consequences of opposing position in physical terms

### Step 4 — Evidence collection (if Justice requests it)

Use /plot evidence to generate requested evidence. Evidence commands run as Bureaucracy
Standing Orders — no Bill or hearing required.

### Step 5 — Clarifying questions (Justice only)

The Justice may ask each attorney one clarifying question.
Print each Q&A clearly labelled:
  JUSTICE → ATTORNEY-A: <question>
  ATTORNEY-A: <answer>

### Step 6 — Ruling

The Justice announces:
- Which position prevails
- The governing physical/empirical basis (Benjamin Franklin Principle)
- The device/hardware outcome protected (Thomas Jefferson Principle)
- Any conditions or constraints on how the ruling is applied

### Step 7 — Record to case law

The prevailing attorney writes the ruling to docs/governance/case_law.md
using the standard case law template. This is a hard gate — implementation cannot
start until the ruling is recorded.

After the ruling is recorded:
- If the ruling enacts a Bill that changes agent scope: invoke agent-updater with the Bill name.
- The Justice reviews and applies any proposed agent edits before implementation begins.

Standard case law entry format:
```
### Case [N]: [Hearing Name]
**Date:** [date]
**Positions:** A — [description] | B — [description]
**Prevailing position:** [A or B]
**Justice's ruling:** [ruling text]
**Physical/empirical basis:** [evidence cited]
**Device outcome protected:** [Thomas Jefferson statement]
**Conditions:** [any constraints on application]
**Enacted bill (if any):** [bill name, or "none"]
**Implementation branch:** [branch name, or "none"]
```

### Nested Hearing Protocol

If a nested hearing must be declared during argument (Step 3–5):
1. Pause the current hearing — print PARENT HEARING PAUSED
2. Complete the nested hearing fully (Steps 1–7)
3. Resume parent hearing — print PARENT HEARING RESUMED
4. The child ruling is new evidence for the parent hearing; do not re-debate it

---

## bill subcommand

Invokes the bill-drafter agent to produce a complete, debate-ready Bill.

What bill-drafter does:
  1. Reads amendments, case law, device_context.md, and relevant source files
  2. Checks evidence gates (physical evidence must exist in the record)
  3. Identifies the correct amendment grounding
  4. Verifies the proposed change is specific and measurable
  5. Outputs a complete Bill or an INCOMPLETE report explaining what evidence is missing

Bill quality gates (all must pass before a Bill is output):
  Evidence gate    — physical evidence must exist in device_context.md or this session
  Amendment gate   — an Article or Amendment must authorise the change
  Outcome gate     — expected improvement must name a domain primitive and unit
  Scope gate       — proposed change must name specific files, functions, or values

After bill-drafter outputs the Bill:
  1. Review the Bill with the Justice
  2. Run /judicial hear "[Bill name]" to open debate
  3. After ruling, implement on the branch named in the Bill

Constitutional grounding:
  Article I  — Bill must trace to a domain primitive
  Article II — Bills are proposed; the Justice enacts
  Amendment 4 — three consecutive failures should trigger a Bill, not a fourth attempt

If no description given for bill subcommand, print usage and stop.

---

Now parse "hear "Amendment 1 sample-rate revision (Bill 001)" "revise per Bill" vs "Position B: metadata-only revision"":
  First word is the subcommand: "hear" or "bill"
  For "hear": invoke the judicial-clerk agent, then run the 7-step hearing procedure.
    Parse remaining args as: first quoted string = hearing name,
    text after first "vs" = position B, text between name and "vs" = position A.
    If parsing fails, print usage and stop.
  For "bill": invoke the bill-drafter agent with the remaining text as the problem description.
    If no description given, print usage and stop.

(Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- code-reviewer: Use this agent to review firmware and algorithm source code for constitutional compliance and quality. Checks Article I traceability (every threshold traces to a domain primitive), FSM structural integrity, filter chain coherence, and unit consistency. Produces a triage report — not a rewrite. (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep)

- codex:codex-rescue: Proactively use when Claude Code is stuck, wants a second implementation or diagnosis pass, needs a deeper root-cause investigation, or should hand a substantial coding task to Codex through the shared runtime (Tools: Bash)

- constitution-auditor: Use this agent to audit the governance record for internal consistency. Checks for orphaned amendments (never cited in case law or source), frozen precedents that conflict with live amendments, toolchain_config alignment with Amendment 3, and amendment index accuracy. Run before any /compact or stage gate. (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep)

- doc-reviewer: Use this agent to audit docs/ for completeness, staleness, and consistency gaps. Checks device_context.md, toolchain_config.md, and governance docs against each other. Produces a gap table — not a rewrite. Run before any stage gate or before /compact. (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep)

- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. - judicial-clerk: Use this agent to warm up the courtroom before any Judicial Hearing. Confirms all hearing agents are present, prints a status line for each, and reports courtroom ready. No tmux. No panel setup. Single terminal only. (Tools: Bash, Read)

- police: Use this agent to detect constitutional violations by agents and by the human engineer. Reads git history, session output, and governance records to find unauthorized changes, scope overruns, Article I/II breaches, and three-strike violations. 1	# Sensor mounting — PVDF, PVDF + proof mass, PZT
2	
3	How you mount each sensor matters at least as much as which sensor you
4	pick. The same chip on the same floor with two different mounts gives
5	different SNR, different bandwidth, and sometimes different *physics*
6	(strain sensor vs accelerometer). This doc covers the three sensor
7	configurations we're using.
8	
9	## TL;DR — the right mount for each, in one line
10	
11	| Sensor | Best mount | Sensing mode | Best at |
12	|---|---|---|---|
13	| **Bare PVDF film** | Bonded flat to the floor (or to a thin metal shim coupled to the floor) with rigid epoxy across the full footprint | Strain — picks up in-plane bending of the floor | Low-frequency floor flexure (1–200 Hz). Cheap. Bad on stiff floors. |
14	| **PVDF + proof mass** | Cantilever or simply-supported beam with the mass at the free end, base bolted (or stiff-epoxied) to the floor | Acceleration — inertial | Surface acceleration up to ~1 kHz. Best general-purpose option for fall detection. |
15	| **PZT disc / ring with proof mass** | Center-bolted or rigid-epoxied to the floor through the metal carrier shim, **inside a shielded enclosure** | Acceleration / strain (depends on geometry) | High sensitivity, high frequencies. Hard to insulate. |
16	
17	## Universal rules (apply to all three)
18	
19	1. **Couple it rigidly to the floor.** Anything compliant between the
20	   sensor and the floor (foam, soft tape, blu-tack, the carpet pile)
21	   acts as a mechanical low-pass filter. You want the sensor to *move
22	   with the floor*, not relative to it.
23	2. **Surface prep.** Clean the mounting area with isopropyl alcohol,
24	   let it dry. Skip the wax / polish layer that's on most marble and
25	   tile floors — it kills adhesion. For temporary deployments, a 50 mm
26	   square of double-sided tape over a degreased patch is acceptable;
27	   for a real run, a thin layer of cyanoacrylate (super glue) or
28	   2-part epoxy is dramatically better.
29	3. **Strain-relieve the cable.** The cable run from the sensor to the
30	   front-end is a microphone — it picks up vibration, drag, and
31	   triboelectric charge if it moves. Glue the first 10 cm of cable
32	   *to the same surface as the sensor* with a separate dot of epoxy
33	   so cable motion doesn't reach the sensor pads.
34	4. **Shield it.** Especially for PZT and bare PVDF (high source
35	   impedance). A grounded copper-foil enclosure — even a folded piece
36	   of kitchen aluminum foil tied to circuit GND — drops mains hum and
37	   nearby switching noise by 10–20 dB. The bad PZT noise floor in
38	   `water_drop_livingroom/EXPERIMENT.md` is a textbook example of what
39	   skipping this costs you.
40	5. **Same mount for the whole experiment.** If you're comparing two
41	   sensors or two surfaces, the mount has to be identical between
42	   recordings. A change in adhesive or torque can move the SNR by
43	   5+ dB on its own.
44	
45	## Bare PVDF film
46	
47	### What it actually senses
48	
49	PVDF film generates a charge proportional to the **strain** along its
50	length. When the floor flexes (bends), the surface fibers stretch and
51	compress, and a film bonded to the surface stretches and compresses
52	with them. This is why PVDF works best for **low-frequency,
53	large-deflection** events — it's a strain sensor, not an accelerometer.
54	
55	### Mounting
56	
57	- **Adhesive** (in order of preference):
58	  1. Thin layer of **2-part epoxy** spread across the entire film
59	     footprint — gives the best strain coupling, full bandwidth.
60	  2. **Cyanoacrylate (super glue)** — quick, almost as good as epoxy,
61	     more brittle long-term.
62	  3. **Double-sided polyimide / Kapton tape** — fine for a 1-day
63	     experiment, but the tape itself shears under high-frequency
64	     content above ~200 Hz, so you lose the upper band.
65	  4. **Avoid:** foam-backed tape, blu-tack, anything compliant.
66	- **Coverage:** the *entire* film must contact the surface uniformly.
67	  Air gaps under any part of the film mean that part of the film
68	  doesn't strain, reducing output (and in extreme cases adding
69	  resonances at the air-pocket frequency).
70	- **Orientation:** PVDF has an anisotropy axis (the "stretch axis"
71	  marked by the manufacturer). Mount with that axis aligned along the
72	  expected direction of largest strain — for floor-flexure detection,
73	  that's usually parallel to the longest unsupported span of the floor
74	  / tile.
75	- **Electrodes / leads:** the silver-printed electrodes are fragile.
76	  Use conductive copper tape with conductive adhesive, or a soldered
77	  wire on a gold-plated pad — never bend the lead near the electrode.
78	- **Sub-strate plate trick:** if direct epoxy to the floor isn't
79	  acceptable (e.g. a marble surface you can't damage), bond the PVDF
80	  to a **0.1–0.3 mm steel or aluminum shim** first, then epoxy the
81	  shim to the floor. The shim couples the floor strain into the film
82	  while letting you remove the assembly cleanly later. Don't go thicker
83	  than ~0.3 mm or the shim stops flexing with the floor.
84	
85	### Pitfalls
86	
87	- **Tape adhesion failure** is the most common silent killer. After
88	  the first few hard impacts the tape partially delaminates at the
89	  edges; SNR drops by 10–20 dB and you don't notice because the
90	  baseline still looks fine. Inspect the edges before each session.
91	- **Cable strumming.** A 50 cm dangling cable will pick up its own
92	  resonance (~10–30 Hz) every time the floor moves. Tape it down.
93	- **Triboelectric noise.** PVDF is also pyroelectric and triboelectric
94	  — touching the film with bare fingers, or moving the leads, generates
95	  spurious charge spikes. Don't handle during a recording.
96	
97	## PVDF with proof mass (PVDF accelerometer)
98	
99	This is the configuration used as `PVDF_mass_*` in
100	`water_drop_livingroom/`. Adding a small mass converts the sensor from
101	a *strain* device into an *inertial* device — the mass resists motion,
102	so when the floor accelerates the PVDF gets bent by the inertia of the
103	mass. Different physics, different mount.
104	
105	### Geometry
106	
107	Two common mechanical configurations:
108	
109	```
110	   Cantilever                         Simply-supported beam
111	  ───────────────                     ───────────────────
112	                                                 
113	   ┌─────────────────┐               ┌──────────────────────┐
114	   │     mass        │               │       mass            │
115	   │                 │               │                       │
116	   ╞═════PVDF════════╡<- free end    ╞═══════PVDF═══════════╡
117	   │                 │               │                       │
118	   ║║║║ base ║║║║║║║║                ║║║                  ║║║
119	   ║║║║║║ floor ║║║║║                ║║║       floor      ║║║
120	```
121	
122	- **Cantilever** (one end clamped, mass at the free end) — higher
123	  sensitivity per gram of mass, lower resonant frequency. Good for
124	  picking up floor accelerations < 200 Hz.
125	- **Simply-supported beam** (both ends clamped, mass in the middle) —
126	  stiffer, higher resonant frequency, lower sensitivity. Good when you
127	  want broader bandwidth and don't mind giving up some output.
128	
129	For a fall-detection use case (event content mostly < 100 Hz on stiff
130	surfaces, < 50 Hz on soft surfaces), **cantilever** is usually the
131	right pick.
132	
133	### Mounting the base
134	
135	The whole point is that the *base* moves with the floor and the *mass*
136	lags behind. So:
137	
138	- **Base coupling: as rigid as possible.** Two-part epoxy across the
139	  entire base footprint, or — better — a small machined aluminum block
140	  bolted (M3) into a threaded insert epoxied to the floor. Removable
141	  and dramatically more rigid than tape. For temporary work, full-area
142	  epoxy directly to a clean surface.
143	- **Don't pinch the PVDF where it transitions from base to free
144	  section.** The transition zone is a stress concentration; if epoxy
145	  squeezes into the active film area, sensitivity drops.
146	
147	### Choosing the mass
148	
149	- A heavier mass → larger PVDF deflection per g of acceleration → more
150	  output, but lower resonant frequency (more bandwidth limit) and more
151	  fragile.
152	- A typical sweet spot for fall-detection on a 25 mm × 8 mm × 28 µm
153	  PVDF strip: **2–10 g** brass or steel mass at the free end. Glue it
154	  on with the same epoxy used elsewhere in the assembly.
155	- The mass material doesn't matter much (density × volume = mass), but
156	  brass / stainless steel are easier to glue to than aluminum (which
157	  oxidizes).
158	
159	### Resonance
160	
161	A cantilevered mass + PVDF is a damped second-order system with a
162	resonance somewhere between 50 and 500 Hz depending on geometry. **You
163	want this resonance well above the band you care about** (so it doesn't
164	ring and color the response), but ideally not so high that you lose
165	all sensitivity in the 10–100 Hz fall band.
166	
167	- Tap-test it before mounting permanently: tap the mass with a pencil,
168	  watch the receiver's plot, look at the dominant frequency in
169	  `peak_snr_gui.py`. If it sits around 200–500 Hz, you're in a good
170	  spot. If it sits at 30 Hz, the mass is too heavy or the cantilever
171	  too long; trim something.
172	
173	### Pitfalls
174	
175	- **Resonance in-band.** If your cantilever rings at 40 Hz, every fall
176	  excites a 40 Hz tone that swamps the actual signal shape. Stiffen
177	  the cantilever (shorter arm or thicker substrate).
178	- **Mass falls off.** Use real epoxy, not super glue, for the mass-to-
179	  PVDF joint — it sees high stress at every impact.
180	- **The base is too compliant.** Tape-mounted bases give the mass and
181	  the floor common-mode motion, killing sensitivity. Epoxy or bolt.
182	
183	## PZT (with proof mass — the `PZT_ringmass` configuration)
184	
185	PZT is much more sensitive per unit deflection than PVDF, but it's:
186	- **brittle** (cracks under shock if not protected),
187	- **high source impedance** (so it picks up every nearby EMI source
188	  unless properly shielded),
189	- **mechanically rigid** (wants to be bolted or rigid-epoxied, not
190	  taped).
191	
192	### The standard form factor
193	
194	The most common cheap PZT element is a **piezo buzzer disc**: a brass
195	shim ~20–35 mm diameter with a ceramic disc bonded to one side. The
196	brass shim acts as the structural carrier (and one electrode); the top
197	of the ceramic is the other electrode. With a small mass added on
198	top of the ceramic, this becomes the `ringmass` accelerometer.
199	
200	### Mounting
201	
202	- **Center-bolt** through the brass shim into a threaded hole or insert
203	  in the floor / a coupling block. Torque just enough to make the
204	  joint solid (~0.2 N·m); over-torquing crushes the ceramic.
205	- If you can't drill: **rigid epoxy** the brass shim to the floor
206	  across its full footprint. Don't tape — PZT mounted on tape rings
207	  uncontrollably and the response is dominated by the tape, not the
208	  floor.
209	- The mass sits on top of the ceramic, glued with epoxy. Same as PVDF:
210	  match mass to the bandwidth you need.
211	
212	### Shielding (the part that matters most)
213	
214	Skipping this is exactly what cost the PZT 16.5 dB of noise floor in
215	`water_drop_livingroom/EXPERIMENT.md`. Don't repeat the mistake.
216	
217	- **Coax cable from sensor to front-end.** Even 30 cm of unshielded
218	  twisted pair will pick up enough hum to bury small signals. RG-178
219	  or any audio-grade thin coax is fine. Solder the shield to circuit
220	  GND only at the front-end side (not at the sensor side) to avoid
221	  ground loops.
222	- **Faraday cage around the sensor.** Wrap the sensor + the first
223	  10 cm of cable in **copper or aluminum foil**, connect the foil to
224	  circuit GND via a short pigtail at the front-end side. Leave a
225	  small access hole only for the cable. The cage doesn't need to
226	  touch the ceramic — air gap is fine — but it must completely
227	  enclose it.
228	- **Front-end input impedance matching.** The PZT's source impedance
229	  is typically 100 kΩ – 10 MΩ at the frequencies of interest. A
230	  charge-amplifier topology (op-amp with a feedback capacitor) is the
231	  textbook front-end. A simple voltage buffer with an LMC6041 or
232	  AD8541 (FET-input, low bias current) also works for large signals.
233	  Don't drive a long cable directly out of the PZT.
234	- **Don't share ground with switchers.** The Pi's USB / 5 V regulator
235	  is a noise source. Run the PZT analog ground separately and merge it
236	  to digital ground at one star point at the front-end — never inside
237	  the PZT enclosure.
238	
239	### Pitfalls
240	
241	- **Cracking under impact.** PZT can survive shock if it's mounted
242	  with strain relief at the lead joints and the mass isn't slamming
243	  into the ceramic edge. After every hard test, inspect for new
244	  cracks (use a magnifier and look for hairlines around the brass-
245	  ceramic perimeter).
246	- **The ceramic is poled** — the polarity of the output depends on
247	  which electrode you pick as ground. If the trace looks "upside
248	  down" relative to the impact, swap the leads.
249	- **Resonant ringing.** PZT discs have very high-Q resonances
250	  (hundreds of Hz to a few kHz). If you see a single tone coloring
251	  every event, you're near a resonance — add a small damping mass or
252	  a viscous adhesive layer between the ceramic and the proof mass.
253	
254	## Mounting decision matrix
255	
256	If you just need to pick a mount in 60 seconds:
257	
258	| You have… | …on this surface | Mount choice |
259	|---|---|---|
260	| Bare PVDF film | wood / vinyl (compliant) | full-area epoxy direct to floor |
261	| Bare PVDF film | marble / tile (stiff) | epoxy to a 0.2 mm shim, then epoxy shim to floor |
262	| PVDF + mass | any | cantilever, base epoxied (or M3-bolted) to floor; tape only for first-pass test |
263	| PZT + mass | any | brass shim epoxied to floor, full Faraday cage + coax to front-end; M3-bolted if drilling allowed |
264	| Anything | a floor you cannot damage | shim + repositionable adhesive (3M VHB tape) accepting ~5 dB SNR loss |
265	
266	## Verifying the mount before recording
267	
268	A 30-second sanity check before every session:
269	
270	1. **Tap test.** Tap the floor 30 cm from the sensor with a pencil
271	   eraser. Live trace should show a clean, fast-decay impulse with a
272	   ringdown shorter than ~50 ms. If it rings for hundreds of ms or
273	   shows multiple harmonic peaks, the mount is resonating — re-mount.
274	2. **Knuckle test.** Knock once on the floor. The trace should hit a
275	   peak quickly and decay. If the peak is delayed (visible "rise"
276	   instead of an instant onset), the mount is compliant — re-mount.
277	3. **Hum test.** With everything connected but no mechanical input,
278	   look at the noise floor. Touch the cable shield; if the noise jumps
279	   markedly, your shield isn't grounded properly. Touch the sensor;
280	   if it spikes, you don't have a Faraday cage on a high-impedance
281	   sensor (PVDF / PZT).
282	4. **Repeat after the first hard impact.** Adhesive bonds settle (and
283	   sometimes partially fail) on the first big shock. Re-do the tap
284	   test after the first 2–3 fall surrogates.
285	
286	If all four pass, the mount is good. If any fail, fix it before
287	recording — you can't fix bad coupling in software.
288

| **PVDF + proof mass** | Cantilever or simply-supported beam with the mass at the free end, base bolted (or stiff-epoxied) to the floor | Acceleration — inertial | Surface acceleration up to ~1 kHz. Best general-purpose option for fall detection. |
| **PZT disc / ring with proof mass** | Center-bolted or rigid-epoxied to the floor through the metal carrier shim, **inside a shielded enclosure** | Acceleration / strain (depends on geometry) | High sensitivity, high frequencies. Hard to insulate. |

## Universal rules (apply to all three)

1. **Couple it rigidly to the floor.** Anything compliant between the
   sensor and the floor (foam, soft tape, blu-tack, the carpet pile)
   acts as a mechanical low-pass filter. You want the sensor to *move
   with the floor*, not relative to it.
2. **Surface prep.** Clean the mounting area with isopropyl alcohol,
   let it dry. Skip the wax / polish layer that's on most marble and
   tile floors — it kills adhesion. For temporary deployments, a 50 mm
   square of double-sided tape over a degreased patch is acceptable;
   for a real run, a thin layer of cyanoacrylate (super glue) or
   2-part epoxy is dramatically better.
3. **Strain-relieve the cable.** The cable run from the sensor to the
   front-end is a microphone — it picks up vibration, drag, and
   triboelectric charge if it moves. Glue the first 10 cm of cable
   *to the same surface as the sensor* with a separate dot of epoxy
   so cable motion doesn't reach the sensor pads.
4. **Shield it.** Especially for PZT and bare PVDF (high source
   impedance). A grounded copper-foil enclosure — even a folded piece
   of kitchen aluminum foil tied to circuit GND — drops mains hum and
   nearby switching noise by 10–20 dB. The bad PZT noise floor in
   `water_drop_livingroom/EXPERIMENT.md` is a textbook example of what
   skipping this costs you.
5. **Same mount for the whole experiment.** If you're comparing two
   sensors or two surfaces, the mount has to be identical between
   recordings. A change in adhesive or torque can move the SNR by
   5+ dB on its own.

## Bare PVDF film

### What it actually senses

PVDF film generates a charge proportional to the **strain** along its
length. When the floor flexes (bends), the surface fibers stretch and
compress, and a film bonded to the surface stretches and compresses
with them. This is why PVDF works best for **low-frequency,
large-deflection** events — it's a strain sensor, not an accelerometer.

### Mounting

- **Adhesive** (in order of preference):
  1. Thin layer of **2-part epoxy** spread across the entire film
     footprint — gives the best strain coupling, full bandwidth.
  2. **Cyanoacrylate (super glue)** — quick, almost as good as epoxy,
     more brittle long-term.
  3. **Double-sided polyimide / Kapton tape** — fine for a 1-day
     experiment, but the tape itself shears under high-frequency
     content above ~200 Hz, so you lose the upper band.
  4. **Avoid:** foam-backed tape, blu-tack, anything compliant.
- **Coverage:** the *entire* film must contact the surface uniformly.
  Air gaps under any part of the film mean that part of the film
  doesn't strain, reducing output (and in extreme cases adding
  resonances at the air-pocket frequency).
- **Orientation:** PVDF has an anisotropy axis (the "stretch axis"
  marked by the manufacturer). Mount with that axis aligned along the
  expected direction of largest strain — for floor-flexure detection,
  that's usually parallel to the longest unsupported span of the floor
  / tile.
- **Electrodes / leads:** the silver-printed electrodes are fragile.
  Use conductive copper tape with conductive adhesive, or a soldered
  wire on a gold-plated pad — never bend the lead near the electrode.
- **Sub-strate plate trick:** if direct epoxy to the floor isn't
  acceptable (e.g. a marble surface you can't damage), bond the PVDF
  to a **0.1–0.3 mm steel or aluminum shim** first, then epoxy the
  shim to the floor. The shim couples the floor strain into the film
  while letting you remove the assembly cleanly later. Don't go thicker
  than ~0.3 mm or the shim stops flexing with the floor.

### Pitfalls

- **Tape adhesion failure** is the most common silent killer. After
  the first few hard impacts the tape partially delaminates at the
  edges; SNR drops by 10–20 dB and you don't notice because the
  baseline still looks fine. Inspect the edges before each session.
- **Cable strumming.** A 50 cm dangling cable will pick up its own
  resonance (~10–30 Hz) every time the floor moves. Tape it down.
- **Triboelectric noise.** PVDF is also pyroelectric and triboelectric
  — touching the film with bare fingers, or moving the leads, generates
  spurious charge spikes. Don't handle during a recording.

## PVDF with proof mass (PVDF accelerometer)

This is the configuration used as `PVDF_mass_*` in
`water_drop_livingroom/`. Adding a small mass converts the sensor from
a *strain* device into an *inertial* device — the mass resists motion,
so when the floor accelerates the PVDF gets bent by the inertia of the
mass. Different physics, different mount.

### Geometry

Two common mechanical configurations:

```
   Cantilever                         Simply-supported beam
  ───────────────                     ───────────────────
                                                 
   ┌─────────────────┐               ┌──────────────────────┐
   │     mass        │               │       mass            │
   │                 │               │                       │
   ╞═════PVDF════════╡<- free end    ╞═══════PVDF═══════════╡
   │                 │               │                       │
   ║║║║ base ║║║║║║║║                ║║║                  ║║║
   ║║║║║║ floor ║║║║║                ║║║       floor      ║║║
```

- **Cantilever** (one end clamped, mass at the free end) — higher
  sensitivity per gram of mass, lower resonant frequency. Good for
  picking up floor accelerations < 200 Hz.
- **Simply-supported beam** (both ends clamped, mass in the middle) —
  stiffer, higher resonant frequency, lower sensitivity. Good when you
  want broader bandwidth and don't mind giving up some output.

For a fall-detection use case (event content mostly < 100 Hz on stiff
surfaces, < 50 Hz on soft surfaces), **cantilever** is usually the
right pick.

### Mounting the base

The whole point is that the *base* moves with the floor and the *mass*
lags behind. So:

- **Base coupling: as rigid as possible.** Two-part epoxy across the
  entire base footprint, or — better — a small machined aluminum block
  bolted (M3) into a threaded insert epoxied to the floor. Removable
  and dramatically more rigid than tape. For temporary work, full-area
  epoxy directly to a clean surface.
- **Don't pinch the PVDF where it transitions from base to free
  section.** The transition zone is a stress concentration; if epoxy
  squeezes into the active film area, sensitivity drops.

### Choosing the mass

- A heavier mass → larger PVDF deflection per g of acceleration → more
  output, but lower resonant frequency (more bandwidth limit) and more
  fragile.
- A typical sweet spot for fall-detection on a 25 mm × 8 mm × 28 µm
  PVDF strip: **2–10 g** brass or steel mass at the free end. Glue it
  on with the same epoxy used elsewhere in the assembly.
- The mass material doesn't matter much (density × volume = mass), but
  brass / stainless steel are easier to glue to than aluminum (which
  oxidizes).

### Resonance

A cantilevered mass + PVDF is a damped second-order system with a
resonance somewhere between 50 and 500 Hz depending on geometry. **You
want this resonance well above the band you care about** (so it doesn't
ring and color the response), but ideally not so high that you lose
all sensitivity in the 10–100 Hz fall band.

- Tap-test it before mounting permanently: tap the mass with a pencil,
  watch the receiver's plot, look at the dominant frequency in
  `peak_snr_gui.py`. If it sits around 200–500 Hz, you're in a good
  spot. If it sits at 30 Hz, the mass is too heavy or the cantilever
  too long; trim something.

### Pitfalls

- **Resonance in-band.** If your cantilever rings at 40 Hz, every fall
  excites a 40 Hz tone that swamps the actual signal shape. Stiffen
  the cantilever (shorter arm or thicker substrate).
- **Mass falls off.** Use real epoxy, not super glue, for the mass-to-
  PVDF joint — it sees high stress at every impact.
- **The base is too compliant.** Tape-mounted bases give the mass and
  the floor common-mode motion, killing sensitivity. Epoxy or bolt.

## PZT (with proof mass — the `PZT_ringmass` configuration)

PZT is much more sensitive per unit deflection than PVDF, but it's:
- **brittle** (cracks under shock if not protected),
- **high source impedance** (so it picks up every nearby EMI source
  unless properly shielded),
- **mechanically rigid** (wants to be bolted or rigid-epoxied, not
  taped).

### The standard form factor

The most common cheap PZT element is a **piezo buzzer disc**: a brass
shim ~20–35 mm diameter with a ceramic disc bonded to one side. The
brass shim acts as the structural carrier (and one electrode); the top
of the ceramic is the other electrode. With a small mass added on
top of the ceramic, this becomes the `ringmass` accelerometer.

### Mounting

- **Center-bolt** through the brass shim into a threaded hole or insert
  in the floor / a coupling block. Torque just enough to make the
  joint solid (~0.2 N·m); over-torquing crushes the ceramic.
- If you can't drill: **rigid epoxy** the brass shim to the floor
  across its full footprint. Don't tape — PZT mounted on tape rings
  uncontrollably and the response is dominated by the tape, not the
  floor.
- The mass sits on top of the ceramic, glued with epoxy. Same as PVDF:
  match mass to the bandwidth you need.

### Shielding (the part that matters most)

Skipping this is exactly what cost the PZT 16.5 dB of noise floor in
`water_drop_livingroom/EXPERIMENT.md`. Don't repeat the mistake.

- **Coax cable from sensor to front-end.** Even 30 cm of unshielded
  twisted pair will pick up enough hum to bury small signals. RG-178
  or any audio-grade thin coax is fine. Solder the shield to circuit
  GND only at the front-end side (not at the sensor side) to avoid
  ground loops.
- **Faraday cage around the sensor.** Wrap the sensor + the first
  10 cm of cable in **copper or aluminum foil**, connect the foil to
  circuit GND via a short pigtail at the front-end side. Leave a
  small access hole only for the cable. The cage doesn't need to
  touch the ceramic — air gap is fine — but it must completely
  enclose it.
- **Front-end input impedance matching.** The PZT's source impedance
  is typically 100 kΩ – 10 MΩ at the frequencies of interest. A
  charge-amplifier topology (op-amp with a feedback capacitor) is the
  textbook front-end. A simple voltage buffer with an LMC6041 or
  AD8541 (FET-input, low bias current) also works for large signals.
  Don't drive a long cable directly out of the PZT.
- **Don't share ground with switchers.** The Pi's USB / 5 V regulator
  is a noise source. Run the PZT analog ground separately and merge it
  to digital ground at one star point at the front-end — never inside
  the PZT enclosure.

### Pitfalls

- **Cracking under impact.** PZT can survive shock if it's mounted
  with strain relief at the lead joints and the mass isn't slamming
  into the ceramic edge. After every hard test, inspect for new
  cracks (use a magnifier and look for hairlines around the brass-
  ceramic perimeter).
- **The ceramic is poled** — the polarity of the output depends on
  which electrode you pick as ground. If the trace looks "upside
  down" relative to the impact, swap the leads.
- **Resonant ringing.** PZT discs have very high-Q resonances
  (hundreds of Hz to a few kHz). If you see a single tone coloring
  every event, you're near a resonance — add a small damping mass or
  a viscous adhesive layer between the ceramic and the proof mass.

## Mounting decision matrix

If you just need to pick a mount in 60 seconds:

| You have… | …on this surface | Mount choice |
|---|---|---|
| Bare PVDF film | wood / vinyl (compliant) | full-area epoxy direct to floor |
| Bare PVDF film | marble / tile (stiff) | epoxy to a 0.2 mm shim, then epoxy shim to floor |
| PVDF + mass | any | cantilever, base epoxied (or M3-bolted) to floor; tape only for first-pass test |
| PZT + mass | any | brass shim epoxied to floor, full Faraday cage + coax to front-end; M3-bolted if drilling allowed |
| Anything | a floor you cannot damage | shim + repositionable adhesive (3M VHB tape) accepting ~5 dB SNR loss |

## Verifying the mount before recording

A 30-second sanity check before every session:

1. **Tap test.** Tap the floor 30 cm from the sensor with a pencil
   eraser. Live trace should show a clean, fast-decay impulse with a
   ringdown shorter than ~50 ms. If it rings for hundreds of ms or
   shows multiple harmonic peaks, the mount is resonating — re-mount.
2. **Knuckle test.** Knock once on the floor. The trace should hit a
   peak quickly and decay. If the peak is delayed (visible "rise"
   instead of an instant onset), the mount is compliant — re-mount.
3. **Hum test.** With everything connected but no mechanical input,
   look at the noise floor. Touch the cable shield; if the noise jumps
   markedly, your shield isn't grounded properly. Touch the sensor;
   if it spikes, you don't have a Faraday cage on a high-impedance
   sensor (PVDF / PZT).
4. **Repeat after the first hard impact.** Adhesive bonds settle (and
   sometimes partially fail) on the first big shock. Re-do the tap
   test after the first 2–3 fall surrogates.

If all four pass, the mount is good. If any fail, fix it before
recording — you can't fix bad coupling in software.

# Stage 1 Baseline — Final Sim-to-Real Result (2026-05-16)

This document records the Stage 1 simulator + classifier performance baseline
at the end of the simulator-only iteration phase. Stage 1 is HELD HERE pending
real data collection (see `docs/data_collection_protocol.md` when written).

---

## TL;DR

The simulator + RandomForest classifier — trained ONLY on synthetic data — achieves
on real bathroom CSVs (30 events across step / catfood-fall / water-drop classes,
distance-resolved at 0.5 / 1.5 / 2.0 m):

| Metric | Value | Target | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sensitivity (catfood fall surrogates → fall) | **6/12 = 50.0%** | ≥ 95% | FAILS |
| FP rate (steps + water bottle drops → fall) | **8/18 = 44.4%** | ≤ 1/week | FAILS |

This is the honest simulator-only ceiling. Any further improvement requires
real training data, not simulator tweaks.

---

## Per-distance per-class breakdown

| Source | Tag | Real meaning | Distance | n | Result | Correct % |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| step_201505 | step | walking (NOT-fall) | 0.5 m | 3 | 2/3 wrongly fall | 33% |
| step_201505 | step | walking | 1.5 m | 3 | 1/3 wrongly fall | 67% |
| step_201505 | step | walking | 2.0 m | 3 | 1/3 wrongly fall | 67% |
| water_201505 | other | water-bottle drop (NOT-fall, rigid object confuser) | 0.5 m | 3 | 2/3 wrongly fall | 33% |
| water_201505 | other | water-bottle drop | 1.5 m | 3 | 1/3 wrongly fall | 67% |
| water_201505 | other | water-bottle drop | 2.0 m | 3 | 1/3 wrongly fall | 67% |
| catfood_201505 | fall | body-fall surrogate (catfood bag) | 0.5 m | 3 | 2/3 caught | 67% |
| catfood_201505 | fall | body-fall surrogate | 1.5m_unblocked (human at far side) | 3 | 1/3 caught | 33% |
| catfood_201505 | fall | body-fall surrogate | 1.5m_blocked (human between) | 3 | 1/3 caught | 33% |
| catfood_201505 | fall | body-fall surrogate | 2.0 m | 3 | 2/3 caught | 67% |

## Key observation: amplitude bias

The detector is biased to call CLOSE/HIGH-AMPLITUDE signals "fall" regardless of
class. Close events of any class get flagged ~67% of the time; far events get
flagged ~33% of the time. The new scale-invariant features
(post_pre_rms_ratio, low/high band fractions) helped on synthetic data but
don't dominate on real data with realistic noise + amplitude variation.

## Body absorption test (5 dB body-in-path attenuation)

The catfood 1.5m group had 6 events split into two experimental conditions:
3 "unblocked" (human at the far side from sensor — clear propagation path)
and 3 "blocked" (human between drop point and sensor — body absorbs signal).

Both groups caught at the same rate (1/3 = 33%). With only 3 events per
condition, the noise on this number is too high to validate or reject the
5 dB body-absorption hypothesis (which is implemented in `fall_trajectory`
as `body_absorption_db=5.0` default). Needs ≥ 10 events per condition.

## What this baseline tells us about simulator iteration

The previous validation result was misinterpreted due to wrong tag-to-class
mapping (commit a201022, 2026-05-15). After user clarifications and a
corrected sim-to-real script (`scripts/sim_to_real_test_v2.py`):

- The simulator + sensor + noise pipeline produces reasonable signals
- The classifier trained on synthetic data has an **amplitude bias** that
  doesn't reflect what real falls look like
- Simulator improvements (multi-impact rebound, body absorption,
  cantilever sensor model) reduced the misinterpretation gap but did
  NOT close the actual classifier shortcoming
- The remaining gap requires real training data; further simulator
  tuning yields diminishing returns

---

## State of the simulator at this baseline

`src/signals.py` (v3, commit 893b865 + later) implements:

| Stage | Component | Evidence type |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Backgrounds | vent (60/120/180 Hz tones), shower (broadband), washer (narrow-band), flush (transient) | LITERATURE + HAND-TUNED amplitudes |
| 2. Events | floor_sim FEA plate model (Kirchhoff, 25 modes, 2 geometries) for impacts; analytical slump | PHYSICS + LITERATURE force ranges (Cavanagh & Lafortune, Robinovitch) |
| 2'. Drop rebound | rigid / bouncy / soft_pkg / shatter patterns | LITERATURE (coefficient of restitution) |
| 2''. Body absorption | 5 dB attenuation on fall_trajectory impacts | EMPIRICAL (catfood drop-human-sensor data, n=3, weak validation) |
| 3. Sensor model | MiniSense 100 cantilever (75 Hz, ζ=0.092) + bias HP (6.5 Hz) | DATASHEET-VERIFIED |
| 4. Noise floor | Real bathroom spectrum (1/f + white + peaks at 25/60/91/120/183 Hz) | EMPIRICAL from bathroom_testing/step_201505.csv |

## State of the classifier

`src/algorithm.py` (commit bda4652 + later) — RandomForest with 13 features:
- 6 per-event physical: peak_amp, total_energy, duration_above_noise_ms,
  spectral_centroid_hz, decay_tau_ms, multi_peak_count
- 5 scale-invariant (added 2026-05-16): pre_event_rms, post_event_rms,
  post_pre_rms_ratio, low_band_energy_frac, high_band_energy_frac
- 2 temporal context: events_in_last_5s, time_since_last_event_s

Trained on 20 seeds × 13 profiles × 2 geometries (small + medium bathroom) =
~1067 events. Tested in v1 on 100 synthetic seeds × 13 profiles × 2 geometries
(89.6% sens, 4.1% FP on synthetic). Tested in v2 on 30 real events across 3
CSVs (50% sens, 44% FP — this baseline).

## 14-profile catalog

| Class | Profile | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| noise (5) | noise_vent, noise_shower, noise_flush, noise_washer_local, noise_washer_neighbor | continuous backgrounds, no events |
| confuser (5) | confuser_step, confuser_drop_phone, confuser_drop_heavy, confuser_drop_glass, walk_in_out | events that aren't falls |
| fall (4) | fall_fast, fall_slump, fall_after_walk, fall_softbody_surrogate | fall events (with -5 dB body absorption) |

## Open simulator gaps (will only be closed with real data)

1. **Amplitude bias in classifier** — features need redesign or real data to overcome
2. **Body-absorption value (5 dB) is a guess** — needs ≥ 10 events per condition to validate
3. **Multi-tile mosaic floor not modeled** — defer to install-time calibration (per generalization strategy in `docs/device_context.md`)
4. **Sensor identity assumption unverified** — task #31 (user visual inspection)
5. **Plate damping / geometry** — defer to install-time calibration (tap test)
6. **Real fall human data unavailable** — surrogates only (catfood bag is closest)

## What needs to happen before Stage 2

Per `docs/device_context.md` Install-Time Calibration Design section:

1. Collect real bathroom recordings with metadata per Case 1 ruling (int_mark,
   transport, measured_rate_hz) from multiple bathrooms (≥ 3 recommended)
2. Add real events to training data alongside synthetic
3. Build install-time calibration scripts (tap test + baseline + walk)
4. Verify deployed sensor identity (task #31)
5. Verify firmware streaming rate (Bill 002 ratified ≥ 1 kHz; INT_MARK=0
   required in deployment)

---

- `src/signals.py` — simulator (FEA + sensor + noise + 14 profiles)
- `src/algorithm.py` — RandomForest classifier (13 features)
- `scripts/sim_to_real_test_v2.py` — corrected sim-to-real test

- `docs/governance/case_law.md` — Case 1 (Bill 001) + Case 2 (Bill 002)
- `docs/governance/bills/` — Bill 001 (enacted, modified) + Bill 002 (enacted)
- `docs/plots/sim_layout_diagram.png` — sensor + event-zone visualization

- `docs/plots/sim_render/` — 26 per-profile signal renderings

## Post-baseline finding (2026-05-16): deployed sensor identity

Task #31 (originally "verify deployed sensor visual inspection", reframed to
"confirm part = MiniSense 100 via BOM/marking") resolved with a significant
result: **the deployed sensor is NOT a MiniSense 100**.

Evidence in `~/Documents/piezo_circuit/`:
- `SENSOR_MOUNTING.md`: deployed sensor is a custom-assembled cantilever —
  25 mm × 8 mm × 28 µm bare PVDF strip + 2–10 g brass/steel proof mass at
  the free end, base epoxied to floor. Stated resonance: "50–500 Hz
  depending on geometry" (not a fixed 75 Hz).
- `PVDF压电采集系统资料/BOM_PVDF压电信号调理系统_2023-02-20.csv`: lists only
  conditioning electronics (CA3140 / MAX44248 front-end, 100 MΩ bias
  resistor R48). No commercial sensor module.
- Zero "MiniSense" hits in original repo. The MiniSense 100 assumption
  originated in our simulator work, not the hardware record.

### Implications

- Simulator's cantilever model (fn=75 Hz, ζ=0.092, 1.1 V/g, 6 V/g at
  resonance) is **calibrated to the wrong reference**. Actual values must
  come from tap-testing the real deployed cantilever.
- Still likely valid: 100 MΩ bias × PVDF source impedance → low-Hz HP
  cutoff order of magnitude; 2nd-order cantilever TF shape; high-Z FET
  front-end. fn / ζ / sensitivity are NOT valid.
- Direction of the gap: actual fn could be anywhere 50–500 Hz, which means
  current sim could either over- or under-state spectral content of events.
- Per CLAUDE.md, changing the sensor model is a simulator parameter change
  → requires a **Bill** (legislative process) before edit. Recorded as a
  known open item, not silently fixed.

### Bill candidates for Stage 1 → Stage 2 entry

1. **Sensor-model recalibration Bill**: replace MiniSense 100 datasheet
   values with measured cantilever fn, ζ, sensitivity from tap test.
   Blocked on: tap-test data collection.
2. **Sensor-spec Amendment**: add cantilever geometry (PVDF dimensions,
   mass) to BOM in `docs/device_context.md` so future calibration is
   traceable.

These Bills should be drafted before Stage 2 starts.

**(a) is the only correct one** — clamp the housing/base, cantilever sticks out into free air.

Reason: the MiniSense 100 is an *inertial* sensor. Its physics is "base moves with floor; tip mass lags behind due to inertia; cantilever bends; PVDF makes voltage proportional to that bending." If the cantilever or tip mass is touching anything, it can't lag relative to the base — the inertial effect is killed and you either get no signal or you turn the device into a strain sensor of whatever's touching the tip (totally different transfer function, datasheet no longer applies).

Practical implications for the STL:
1. **Base footprint** (the small PCB the cantilever sticks out of) → clamp this firmly, full contact, against the bottom plate. This is what gets coupled to the floor.
2. **Cantilever beam + tip mass** → must have free air around it. Typical MiniSense needs ~3 mm clearance above and below the beam for full deflection range under shock.
3. **Top plate** → only touches the base, not the cantilever. Easiest way to guarantee this: top plate has a *recess* or *cutout* directly above the cantilever so the beam swings into the void.
4. **200 g preload** → sits on top plate, presses down on base only, never on the beam.

content.text:
(Couldn't render the STEP solid — no CAD libs installed locally and the point cloud alone is just NURBS control points, not the actual mesh. Skipping for now; a screenshot from your CAD tool resolves it instantly if needed.)

On your two design questions:

## Contact area with the ground — **smaller, but with two constraints**

The driver isn't "more contact = better signal." It's the opposite, with caveats.

**Smaller (good) because:**
- **Stay inside one tile**, never bridge a grout joint. Joints are mechanical discontinuities — two tiles next to each other move *differently*, and a plate spanning the joint introduces rocking modes that have nothing to do with the floor and everything to do with your mount. This dominates the answer.
- A small, thick plate keeps its own bending resonance way above the band of interest. A 30 mm aluminum disc 3 mm thick has its first plate mode > 5 kHz. A 100 mm thin plate can ring at a few hundred Hz, right in our band.
- Point-like sensing = better spatial resolution for nearby events.

**Not too small because:**
- Needs full uniform contact — no rocking on a rim. Real tile surfaces have small bumps/dish; a 10 mm dot can rock, a 30 mm patch sits flat.
- Adhesion / preload load gets concentrated to high pressure on a tiny area, which can mark soft tiles.

**Sweet spot: ~25–50 mm in the largest dimension, single-tile only.** Your STEP file's ~30 mm footprint is exactly right.

## Preload weight — **200 g is fine; don't overthink it**

The role of preload is *only* to guarantee full contact (no lift-off, no rock). It is **not** changing the sensor's transfer function as long as the contact is hard-on-hard (your plate is rigid, the tile is rigid — no foam in between).

Quick numbers:
- **Lift-off threshold:** floor acceleration would need to exceed 1 g *downward* to make a free-resting plate float. Bathroom events including falls peak well under 1 g at the floor. So even **50 g would prevent lift-off** in normal operation.
- **Follow-the-floor resonance:** the base assembly + contact stiffness forms a 2nd-order system. With 200 g + a rigid hard-on-hard contact (~10⁷–10⁸ N/m stiffness), the assembly's own resonance is around **1 kHz** — well above the 200 Hz top of our band. The sensor base faithfully tracks floor motion. At 2 kg you'd still be at ~350 Hz (getting close, but ok). Under 50 g you start to risk the resonance creeping into the sensitive band.
- **Damping:** *only* matters if there's a compliant layer (rubber, foam, tape) between weight and plate. Direct steel/lead-on-plastic-housing: zero added damping.

**Anywhere in 100–500 g works equivalently. 200 g is in the sweet spot — heavy enough for forgiving deploy on imperfect tile, light enough to carry around.** Don't put time into tuning this number.

What *does* matter much more than the weight:
1. **Rigid contact path** — no foam, no thick double-sided tape between weight ↔ top plate ↔ base ↔ floor. Soft layers anywhere here become the dominant mechanical filter.
2. **Weight loosely placed (not bonded)** — so install/uninstall is repeatable. As long as it's gravity-loaded onto a rigid stack, no glue needed.

If you want to be precise about it later, the install-time **tap test** will tell you immediately: tap the floor 30 cm from the mount, look at the ringdown. Clean fast decay (< 50 ms) = mount is good. Long ringing = something compliant in the stack, fix the mount.

content.text:
Got it — readable now.

**What I'm seeing (35.5 × 35.5 × 22.65 mm overall):**

| Layer (z) | Feature |
|---|---|
| -8 to -5 mm | **Square baseplate** ~35×35 mm, ~3 mm thick — this is the floor-contact face |
| -5 to +10 mm | **Bracket / vertical slot** — two parallel walls forming a card-slot, holds the MiniSense PCB upright |
| +10 to +14.5 mm | **Cylindrical cap/cup** ~30 mm diameter — top surface for the 200 g weight to sit on |
| Top view slots | Two narrow parallel slots cut through the cap, aligned with the bracket below |

This is the right architecture: rigid floor coupling → rigid PCB clamp → rigid top platform for the preload. Three rigid bodies stacked, one rigid path from weight down to floor — exactly what you want.

**The one thing I can't confirm from the views — and it's the only thing that matters for sensor-model validity:**

Where does the MiniSense cantilever tip end up inside this housing, and does it have free air around it?

Specifically:
1. **PCB orientation:** Is the cantilever pointing **up** (free end inside the cylindrical cap cavity), **down** (free end into the baseplate region), or **horizontal** (parallel to floor)?
2. **Clearance around the tip mass:** The cantilever needs ≥ 2–3 mm of free air on all sides. If the cap underside, the bracket walls, or the baseplate top are within 1 mm of the tip mass, the cantilever can't deflect → no signal, OR it bottoms out on hard impacts (clipping + nonlinear damping).
3. **What are the two narrow slots in the cap for?** If they're a window into the cap cavity that the cantilever points into, perfect. If they're just lead-access slots and the cantilever sits in an enclosed pocket somewhere else, I need to see where that pocket is.

One quick check you can do: load the STEP into your CAD and section-cut through the cantilever plane. If you can see the cantilever inside the assembly with empty space around it, you're good. If anything touches the tip mass at rest (or comes within ~1 mm), reshape that pocket before printing.

Otherwise the mount looks correct. 35 mm baseplate is well under a standard 200 mm bathroom tile, so no joint-bridging risk. The cap is a clean platform for the 200 g.

## Install-Time Calibration Design (planned, Stage 2/3 deliverable)

To generalize across the wide variation in real bathrooms (tile size,
bonding, subfloor, wall coupling, ambient noise, sensor placement),
the device performs a one-time install calibration. This is the
generalization strategy of record per 2026-05-16 — the simulator does
NOT need to model every bathroom variation accurately; the install
calibration captures the actual deployment's response.

**Three-step install calibration:**

| Step | Duration | What is measured | How algorithm uses it |
|------|----------|------------------|------------------------|
| 1. Quiet baseline | 60 s | Ambient noise floor RMS + spectrum (vent, plumbing, washer if present) | Set adaptive event-detection thresholds; baseline-RMS becomes the denominator for SNR-based features |
| 2. Tap test at 3 distances | ~2 min | Impulse response at known xy positions (e.g., 0.5 m, 1.5 m, 2.5 m from sensor) | Measures actual plate damping, spatial decay rate, local tile resonance, and bonding state — ALL bathroom-specific physics in one measurement |
| 3. Calibration walk | ~1 min | Real footstep signature at moderate pace | Confirms walking-discriminator features work in this bathroom; sets reference amplitude for "normal walking" used by adaptive thresholds |

**What this absorbs:**
- Multi-tile mosaic effects (lateral grout damping)
- Tile size + bonding state (local response in step 2)
- Subfloor variation (slab vs joist appears as different impulse response shape)
- Wall coupling (affects boundary modes captured in step 2)
- Vent / washer locations (captured in step 1 baseline)
- Sensor placement xy (implicit — the IR is from the sensor's actual location)

**What the algorithm requires to leverage calibration:**
- Adaptive event thresholds (MAD-based, already in `src/algorithm.py`)
- Scale-invariant features for classification (band fractions, ratios — partially in features; could be extended)
- Calibration-derivable amplitude reference (e.g., "fall energy ≥ K × measured-walking-energy" instead of "≥ X mg")
- Decay-time reference relative to plate signature ("post-event RMS returns to baseline in ≤ N × plate-ringdown-tau" instead of "≤ M ms")

The first two are in scope for the algorithm as it stands. The third
and fourth would be a feature-engineering pass at Stage 2/3, after
real calibration-measurement data is available.

**Simulator implications:**

This calibration strategy makes most per-bathroom simulator detail
unnecessary:
- Multi-tile mosaic modeling — defer (calibration captures lateral
  grout damping)
- Exact plate-damping value — defer (calibration measures the actual
  damping in tap test)
- Exact bathroom geometry — defer (calibration captures spatial decay)
- Furniture mass loading — defer (captured in baseline)

The simulator IS still needed for:
- Algorithm development (representative-enough signals to validate logic)
- Structural physics that's bathroom-independent (multi-impact rebound,
  body-fall multi-stage signature, slow-slump dynamics, sensor model)

This re-prioritizes the simulator-improvement roadmap toward STRUCTURAL
features and away from per-bathroom parameter accuracy.

---

## Signal Inventory

| Signal | Physical quantity | Unit | Normal range | Hard limits | Sample rate | Primitive |
|--------|------------------|------|--------------|-------------|-------------|-----------|
| Piezo (PVDF+mass) | Floor acceleration | m/s² (derived from V via charge-amp transfer function) | ±0.5 g typical bathroom activity | clip at front-end rail (≈ ±5 V at ADC input) | Active firmware: INT_MARK-dependent (default 0 → ~1.9 kHz; INT_MARK=1 → 500 Hz). Must be INT_MARK=0 to satisfy P1's ≥ 1 kHz clause | P1 |
| Microphone — broadband channel | Acoustic pressure | Pa (or 16-bit PCM count) | 30–80 dB SPL room ambient | clip at digital full-scale | 8–16 kHz (TBD at /toolchain init) | P2 |
| Microphone — speech-band channel | Acoustic pressure (300–3400 Hz) | Pa (or 16-bit PCM count) | response-time speech bursts | clip at digital full-scale | derived from broadband channel | P2 |
| WiFi sensing | Human room occupancy | boolean (+ optional confidence 0–1) | 0 or 1 with confidence ≥ 0.7 stable | sensor-not-responding watchdog | event-driven or 1 Hz poll (TBD) | P3 |

**Stretch / cost-gated sensors (deferred to /toolchain init decision):**
- PIR — only if WiFi-sensing presence proves unreliable in bathroom RF environment
- IMU on device housing — only if device housing itself gets bumped causing piezo false positives
- MLX thermal — likely too expensive; skip

**Pre-existing assets carried in from `~/Documents/piezo_circuit/`:**
- Charge-amplifier front-end (CA3140 or MAX44248, 100 MΩ ∥ 10 nF feedback)
- Sensor-mounting protocol (`SENSOR_MOUNTING.md` — PVDF+mass cantilever, full-area epoxy)

- Sensor-mounting protocol (`SENSOR_MOUNTING.md` — PVDF+mass cantilever, full-area epoxy) — superseded by the housing design below for piezo_fall

**Deployment-specific sensor housing (piezo_fall):**

CAD file: `~/Documents/piezo_circuit/ground_cantilever_housing.{stp,stl}`
(user-designed, 2026-05-16, confirmed correct via review).

Architecture: 3 rigid sections stacked along Z, single rigid load path
from preload weight → top platform → PCB clamp → baseplate → floor.

| Section | Z range (mm) | Function |
|---------|-------------|----------|
| Baseplate | -8 to -5 | Square 35×35 mm, ~3 mm thick — flat ground contact. Single-tile sized (well under standard 200 mm bathroom tile, no grout-joint bridging). |
| PCB clamp / bracket | -5 to +10 | Through-slot grips MiniSense PCB edges. Pins/connectors route out top and bottom of the slot. Cantilever projects into the housing interior cavity with free air on all sides — no contact with walls or cap. |
| Top platform / cap | +10 to +14.5 | Cylindrical disc ~30 mm diameter, flat top — surface for the 200 g preload weight to sit on. |

**Preload:** ~200 g loose weight resting on top platform. Not bonded —
removable for transport, repeatable on re-install. Range 100–500 g all
acceptable; the figure isn't precision-critical.

**Why this preserves the datasheet sensor model:**

- Cantilever has free air around the tip mass → 2nd-order dynamics
  (fn ≈ 75 Hz, ζ ≈ 0.092) preserved. No clamping → no resonance shift.
- Rigid hard-on-hard load path (PLA/PETG print → MiniSense PCB →
  baseplate → tile) → base-on-floor follow-the-floor resonance well
  above 1 kHz. Faithful floor tracking in the 0–200 Hz band of interest.
- 35 mm baseplate within one tile → no inter-tile rocking modes.

**What still needs install-time tap-test verification:**

Even with a correct housing design, the *as-deployed* coupling depends
on tile flatness, dust, the specific tile, and operator placement.
The 30-second tap test in step 2 of the install calibration above
validates: tap 30 cm from sensor → expect clean impulse with ringdown
< 50 ms. Long ringing or delayed rise = compliant contact, fix the
deploy before recording.

# Data Collection Protocol — Stage 1 → Stage 2 Bridge

**Status:** Draft 2026-05-16. Approved-to-execute pending Article II
human go-ahead on each session (each recording session is a Stage 2
gate prerequisite, not a Standing Order).

**Purpose:** Bridge Stage 1's simulator-only baseline (50% sensitivity /
44% FP per `docs/stage_1_baseline.md`) to a real-data corpus that
Stage 2 can train and validate against.

This protocol bundles three things that share the same hardware setup,
so you only deploy the device once per session:

1. **Mount sanity check** (per-session, ~1 min) — confirms the housing
   is properly seated on the tile
2. **Install-time calibration capture** (per-bathroom, ~5 min) — the
   3-step calibration in `docs/device_context.md` Install-Time
   Calibration Design
3. **Labeled event collection** (per-bathroom, 15–60 min) — the actual
   training/validation data

---

## Hardware

- **Device under test:** STM32F103C8T6 + MiniSense 100 in the
  ground_cantilever_housing (CAD: `~/Documents/piezo_circuit/`)
- **Preload:** ~200 g weight on top platform
- **Firmware:** active build at `~/Documents/piezo_circuit/代码 - 调节发送频率/USER/main.c`
  with **INT_MARK = 0** (mandatory — satisfies Amendment 1 P1 ≥ 1 kHz
  rate floor per Case 1+2)
- **Transport:** USB-USART2 (USART2 PA2/PA3, 115200 baud, FireWater
  ASCII `%.3f\n`)
- **Sample-rate check:** before any recording, capture 10 s of UART
  output, count lines, compute measured_rate_hz. Must be ≥ 1000 Hz
  per Amendment 1 P1. If less, abort — INT_MARK is wrong or buffer
  is dropping.

**Mandatory CSV metadata** (per Case 1 ruling, CSVs missing these are
**not admissible as Article I evidence**):

```
# int_mark: 0
# transport: USART2_USB
# measured_rate_hz: <actual measured rate, e.g. 1380>
# bathroom_id: <e.g. "bathroom_A_main">
# tile_size_mm: <approx, e.g. 200x200>
# device_xy_in_room: <e.g. "0.3m from west wall, 0.5m from south wall">
# operator: <name>
# date: YYYY-MM-DD
# session_id: <unique>
```

---

## Session 0: Per-session mount sanity check (~1 min)

Goal: catch a bad deploy before wasting 30 minutes on a session that
turns out to have a compliant contact.

1. Place housing on tile. Confirm baseplate is flush — no rocking when
   you push the cap with a finger.
2. Place 200 g weight on top platform.
3. Start UART capture.
4. **Tap test:** with a fingernail or pencil eraser, tap the tile
   30 cm from the housing. Repeat 5 times with ~2 s between taps.
5. Stop capture. Visually inspect (plot or scope):
   - **Pass:** clean impulse, ringdown < 50 ms, no visible oscillation
     between taps
   - **Fail (re-seat):** ringdown > 200 ms (compliant contact), or
     delayed rise (foam in path), or large oscillation between taps
     (loose preload or rocking baseplate)

If the sanity check fails, re-clean the tile surface (alcohol wipe,
remove dust/wax), re-seat the housing, repeat.

---

## Session 1: Install-time calibration (~5 min, once per bathroom)

Per `docs/device_context.md` Install-Time Calibration Design.

### Step 1A: Quiet baseline (60 s)

- Operator leaves bathroom, no water running
- Record 60 s of UART
- Save as `<bathroom_id>_baseline_<YYYYMMDD>.csv`
- Purpose: noise floor RMS + spectrum (vent, plumbing, distant
  appliances), becomes the SNR denominator

### Step 1B: Tap test at 3 distances (~2 min)

For each distance ∈ {0.5 m, 1.5 m, 2.5 m} from sensor:
- Mark the tap location with tape so it's repeatable
- Operator stands at that distance, taps floor 5 times with a fingertip,
  ~2 s between taps
- Save as `<bathroom_id>_tap_<distance>m_<YYYYMMDD>.csv`
- Purpose: impulse response per distance → plate damping, spatial
  decay rate, local tile resonance, bonding state

### Step 1C: Calibration walk (~1 min)

- Operator walks normally around the bathroom for 60 s, varying paths
- Save as `<bathroom_id>_walk_<YYYYMMDD>.csv`
- Purpose: real footstep signature → reference amplitude for "normal
  walking" used by adaptive thresholds

---

## Session 2: Labeled event collection (15–60 min, repeat per bathroom)

### Event classes to collect (per `docs/device_context.md` Simulation Profile Catalog)

| Class | Event | Target count per bathroom | Notes |
|-------|-------|---------------------------|-------|
| **fall** | catfood-bag drop, body-fall surrogate | ≥ 30 events | At each of 0.5 / 1.5 / 2.5 m, both with and without body-in-path between drop and sensor (per drop-human-sensor finding) |
| **fall** | slow-slump surrogate (heavy bag lowered onto floor) | ≥ 10 events | Slow controlled descent, not free fall |
| **fall** | actual human fall (controlled — onto mat, by operator) | as many as you're willing | Highest-value data. Mat reduces injury but distorts signal — flag mat-cushioned events in metadata. |
| confuser | normal step (walking) | ≥ 30 events (built into walk in 1C) | |
| confuser | water bottle drop (rigid object) | ≥ 15 events at 0.5 / 1.5 / 2.5 m | |
| confuser | object drop — phone | ≥ 10 events | Same distances |
| confuser | object drop — glass (be careful) | ≥ 10 events | Same distances |
| confuser | walk-in / walk-out (operator entering/leaving) | ≥ 5 transitions | |
| noise | shower running | 60 s continuous | |
| noise | vent on | 60 s continuous | |
| noise | toilet flush | 5 flushes | |
| noise | washer (if in or adjacent to bathroom) | 60 s + spin-up/spin-down | |

### Logging discipline

For each event during recording:
- Operator says event name out loud immediately at impact (optional —
  helps when manually segmenting later)
- After each event-block, record:
  - Event class label
  - Distance from sensor (m)
  - Body-in-path? (yes/no)
  - Surface state (wet/dry)
  - Any anomaly (e.g., bottle bounced off wall first)

A simple paper or phone-notes log with timestamps is sufficient. The
goal is to be able to label each event in the CSV after the session.

---

## Output

Per bathroom, expected files:
```
<bathroom_id>_baseline_<date>.csv          # Session 1A
<bathroom_id>_tap_0.5m_<date>.csv          # Session 1B
<bathroom_id>_tap_1.5m_<date>.csv
<bathroom_id>_tap_2.5m_<date>.csv
<bathroom_id>_walk_<date>.csv              # Session 1C
<bathroom_id>_events_<session_n>_<date>.csv  # Session 2 — can be split across runs
<bathroom_id>_log.md                        # event-label log (handwritten OK)
```

Store under `data/<bathroom_id>/` in this repo. Each CSV must include
the metadata header block specified above.

---

## Stage 2 entry criteria (what "enough data" means)

Stage 2 can open when:
- At least 1 bathroom has full install-calibration + ≥ 60 labeled
  events across the catalog (≥ 30 fall surrogates, ≥ 30 confusers)
- All CSVs include the mandatory metadata header
- A held-out test set is identified (e.g., 1 of 3 bathrooms reserved
  for final evaluation, never seen by classifier training)

The classifier retraining + sim-to-real v3 happens after this gate.
A Bill drafted at Stage 2 entry will propose the specific train/val/test
split and the simulator changes (if any) needed once real data exposes
the actual gaps in the synthetic distribution.

---

## What is NOT in scope for this protocol

- **Actual unassisted human falls** — too dangerous outside a controlled
  setting. The catfood-bag and bag-lowering surrogates plus mat-cushioned
  controlled falls cover the simulator's "fall" class.
- **Multi-occupant scenarios** — Stage 3 or later.
- **Multi-bathroom IRL generalization test** — Stage 3.
- **Long-duration unattended recording** — Stage 3 (need a separate
  storage / battery review first).

---

## Open questions before first execution

1. **Sample-rate measurement procedure**: should the rate-check be a
   one-shot count on a dedicated 10 s capture, or inline metadata on
   every recording? (Recommend: inline — record start/stop wall clock
   timestamps + line count in CSV header.)
2. **Storage path:** create `data/` directory in this repo, or store
   outside the repo (large CSVs may bloat git)? Recommend: store outside
   repo, symlink, .gitignore the symlink target.
3. **Backup:** the catfood/water/step CSVs from `~/Documents/piezo_circuit/bathroom_testing/`
   should be migrated into the same `data/` tree with metadata headers
   retro-fitted (operator best-effort) so they're admissible.

content.text:
**Material: PLA** (PETG as second choice).

Why: the housing's job is to be a rigid extension of the floor. You want **high stiffness, low damping**.
- PLA: stiffness ~3.5 GPa, loss factor ~0.01 (very low damping) — acts almost like a rigid solid in the band of interest. Cheap, easy print, dimensionally stable. Brittle, but this part takes zero impact loads.
- PETG: slightly less stiff, slightly more damping, but tougher. Use if you've had PLA crack on a tight PCB clamp fit.
- **Don't use:** TPU/TPE (soft — destroys the whole point), nylon (absorbs moisture in bathroom → swells/changes dim), ABS (warping pain for no benefit here).
- Resin SLA also fine if you have a printer — it's stiff and naturally solid.

**Infill: print it solid (100%).**

For a part this small (~15 g of filament at 100% — you're saving almost nothing by going sparse), the mechanical penalties of hollow are not worth it:
- The cap and baseplate carry concentrated load (preload above, sensor + floor below). Sparse infill = the top/bottom layers can flex under the 200 g load → introduces compliance that becomes part of the mechanical filter, exactly what we don't want.
- Internal voids (sparse infill) add minute damping from air-pocket resonance / cavity acoustics. Tiny effect, but for a "pure follower" mount, you want zero.
- Solid PLA's mass-to-stiffness ratio gives the lowest follow-the-floor compliance per gram.

If you absolutely want to save filament: keep **100% infill in the baseplate region (Z < 0) and the top cap region (Z > +10)**, and allow ~50% in the middle bracket walls (they're not load-bearing in the floor-following direction). But honestly, for a 30 mm housing, just go 100% everywhere.

**Two practical settings that matter as much as material/infill:**

1. **Perimeters / walls: 4–5** (not the default 2–3). Most of the stiffness in a small FDM part comes from perimeters, not infill. Thicker walls beat denser infill for the same filament use.
2. **Print orientation: baseplate flat on build plate, housing growing upward.** This puts the FDM layer lines *horizontal*, so the vertical preload load compresses the layers (strongest direction). Printing on its side puts the load into layer-to-layer adhesion (weakest direction).
3. **First layer matters** — the bottom of the baseplate is your floor contact face. Print on a smooth build plate (smooth PEI / glass), confirm the first layer is flat with no warp or elephant's foot. If the baseplate's bottom is convex by 0.3 mm, you've introduced a rocker — exactly the failure the install tap-test is meant to catch, but better to not introduce it in the first place.

TL;DR: **PLA, 100% infill, 4 walls, baseplate down on the build plate, smooth bed.**

---

Now back to the protocol I just drafted — `docs/data_collection_protocol.md` is written and the housing spec is appended to `docs/device_context.md`. Want me to commit both before the print discussion sidetracks us further?

message.content: what about ABS / ABS-CF those?

content.text:
**ABS: worse, don't bother.**

Compared to PLA for *this* use case:
- Stiffness: ~2.2 GPa vs PLA's ~3.5 GPa — **less stiff**, exactly the wrong direction
- Damping: loss factor ~0.025 vs PLA's ~0.01 — **more damping**, also wrong direction
- Print pain: warping, needs enclosure, smelly
- Its one advantage (Tg ~105°C vs PLA's ~60°C) doesn't matter here — a bathroom never gets close to 60°C, even with shower steam at floor level

ABS is the right pick for hot car-interior parts or tool handles. For a vibration-coupling housing it's a downgrade.

**ABS-CF (or any CF-filled): better on paper, but the gain is wasted here.**

ABS-CF and friends (PLA-CF, PETG-CF, PA-CF):
- Stiffness: ~5–8 GPa (2–3× plain plastic) — **stiffer**, good
- Damping: loss factor ~0.005–0.01 — similar to PLA, also good
- Dimensional stability: excellent (CF kills shrinkage)
- Cost: 2–3× PLA price
- Needs hardened nozzle ($15–20 if you don't already have one)
- Brittle (more so than plain), surface is matte/granular

The thing is: we already calculated that 200 g preload + PLA gives a follow-the-floor resonance around **1 kHz**, well above our 200 Hz upper band. Going to ABS-CF pushes that to ~1.5–2 kHz. That's nice in principle but invisible at the signal level — we're already in the "perfect follower" regime with PLA. The sensor model, ambient noise, and tile-to-tile variation are the real bottlenecks, not housing stiffness.

**The honest matrix:**

| Material | Mechanically | Practical | Verdict for this part |
|---|---|---|---|
| **PLA** | Stiff (3.5 GPa), low damping | Cheap, easy, no enclosure needed | **Recommended.** Sufficient. |
| PETG | A bit less stiff, a bit more damping, tougher | Easy print, won't crack on tight fits | Fine alternative. |
| ABS | Less stiff than PLA, more damping | Warp, fumes, enclosure | Don't. |
| ABS-CF | Very stiff (~6 GPa), low damping, stable | 2-3× cost, hardened nozzle needed | Only if you have it on the shelf already. Pay-for-overkill. |
| PLA-CF / PETG-CF | Same story as ABS-CF | Same | Same — overkill. |
| Resin (SLA) | Stiff, naturally solid | Brittle, post-processing | Fine if you have an SLA printer set up. |

**TL;DR:** PLA is the right call. ABS-CF is a "well, technically better" answer that costs 3× and changes nothing measurable at the output. Use it if you happen to have a spool and a hardened nozzle; otherwise the boring choice wins.
